items.descriptionOriginal: Η διαχείριση βάρους περιλαμβάνει ένα εξατομικευμένο θεραπευτικό πλάνο αντιμετώπισης που μπορεί να βασίζεται σε αλλαγές στον τρόπο ζωής και διατροφής και φαρμακευτική αγωγή. Στις 3 Νοεμβρίου 2026, το Χαροκόπειο Πανεπιστήμιο ξεκίνησε το «My NutriPath», μια δωρεάν υπηρεσία τηλεσυμβουλευτικής με διαιτολόγο-διατροφολόγο για ασθενείς που ξεκινούν θεραπεία με οποιαδήποτε από τις διαθέσιμες εγκεκριμένες ενέσιμες αγωγές για τη διαχείριση της νόσου της παχυσαρκίας. Η υπηρεσία υλοποιείται με την χορηγική υποστήριξη της Φαρμασέρβ-Λίλλυ. Κάθε άτομο με παχυσαρκία που θα εντάσσεται στο My NutriPath, θα λαμβάνει 5 συνεδρίες τηλεσυμβουλευτικής μέσα στους πρώτους 6 μήνες, με εξατομικευμένο διατροφικό πλάνο, εκπαίδευση για βιώσιμες αλλαγές στον τρόπο ζωής του και καθοδήγηση προσαρμοσμένη στις ιδιαίτερες ανάγκες και στους θεραπευτικούς του στόχους. Θα ακολουθεί μία επιπλέον τηλεφωνική συνεδρία αξιολόγησης στον πρώτο χρόνο από την ένταξή του στην υπηρεσία. Η υπηρεσία αφορά ασθενείς σε κάθε ενέσιμη αγωγή που ενδείκνυται για την αντιμετώπιση της παχυσαρκίας. Η παραπομπή γίνεται από τον θεράποντα ιατρό κατά την έναρξη της θεραπείας, σύμφωνα με τις εγκεκριμένες δόσεις έναρξης, και προϋποθέτει ΔΜΣ ≥ 30 kg/m² ή ΔΜΣ ≥ 27 και < 30 kg/m² με τουλάχιστον μία συννοσηρότητα (πχ υπέρταση, δυσλιπιδαιμία, αποφρακτική υπνική άπνοια, καρδιαγγειακή νόσο, προδιαβήτη ή σακχαρώδη διαβήτη τύπου 2). Με το My NutriPath, οι ασθενείς θα έχουν πρόσβαση σε εξειδικευμένο διαιτολόγο-διατροφολόγο, που θα τους καθοδηγεί με ένα εξατομικευμένο διατροφικό πλάνο. Η υποστήριξη αυτής της πρωτοβουλίας από την Φαρμασέρβ-Λίλλυ, ενισχύει μια πιο ολιστική προσέγγιση στη φροντίδα του ασθενούς με παχυσαρκία, συνδυάζοντας την υγιεινοδιαιτητική παρέμβαση με την φαρμακευτική αντιμετώπιση. Ειδήσεις σήμερα Διατροφικές διαταραχές: Στο επίκεντρο η προστασία παιδιών και εφήβων Ιλαρά: 5 σοβαρές επιπλοκές που πρέπει να γνωρίζουν οι γονείς – Ο παιδίατρος εξηγεί Εμμηνόπαυση: Ποια ευρωπαϊκή χώρα καθιερώνει αναρρωτική άδεια με αποδοχές – Το μεγάλο κενό στην Ελλάδα

items.descriptionOriginal: Every October, something extraordinary happens in the Maldives. Millions of dragonflies begin appearing across the islands, even though there is hardly any freshwater for them to breed in. Where are they coming from? Scientists believe many of these tiny travellers arrive from India, crossing hundreds of kilometres of open sea. Some may even continue their journey towards Africa. And here's what makes this so fascinating. The globe skimmer dragonfly ( Pantala flavescens ), also called the wandering glider, measures barely five centimetres and weighs around 300 milligrams. That's less than a gram! Yet this tiny insect may undertake one of the most remarkable journeys in the animal world, travelling thousands of kilometres with help from something familiar to all of us in India: the monsoon. But how does an insect so small cross an ocean without stopping? And why would it attempt such a journey in the first place? Scientists have spent years trying to answer these questions. The mystery of millions of dragonflies arriving in the Maldives In 2009, researcher R Charles Anderson published a study about something that had puzzled observers in the Maldives for years. Every October, enormous numbers of dragonflies appeared on the islands. But the Maldives has very little surface freshwater, making it an unlikely place for dragonflies to complete their life cycle. By studying when the insects appeared in India and the Maldives, Anderson found evidence suggesting they were travelling from southern India, covering approximately 500 to 1,000 kilometres. His findings, published in the Journal of Tropical Ecology , raised an even bigger possibility. What if the Maldives was simply one stop on a much longer journey towards East Africa? The answer appeared to be connected to the changing monsoon. It all begins with something as simple as a rain-filled puddle To understand why these dragonflies travel, we first need to understand where they raise their young. Many dragonflies lay their eggs in ponds and lakes. The globe skimmer has an unusual advantage: it can breed in temporary pools formed by rainfall. Think of the shallow puddles that appear in fields, open grounds and low-lying areas during India's monsoon. For this dragonfly, these pools can become nurseries. The female lays her eggs in the water, where the young dragonflies develop before emerging as adults. But these pools do not last forever. Once the rains stop, they begin drying up. So, as rainfall shifts from one region to another, the dragonflies move towards places where fresh water becomes available. India's southwest monsoon, which generally lasts from June to September, creates ideal breeding opportunities. And when the rains begin moving southwards, the dragonflies appear to follow. Measuring around five centimetres and weighing less than a gram, it is among the world's most widely distributed dragonflies. Photograph: (Bangalore Mirror) How can something weighing less than a gram fly across an ocean? Here's where the story becomes even more remarkable. If a dragonfly tried to cross the Indian Ocean by constantly beating its wings, it would soon run out of energy. So how does it manage? It may be doing something similar to what birds do: using favourable winds to help carry it forward. Anderson's research suggested that the insects travel with winds associated with a shifting band of clouds and rainfall near the equator. Scientists call this the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone, or ITCZ. Simply put, it is a region where winds meet, creating changing weather patterns. As this region moves southwards after India's monsoon, it can bring winds that favour the dragonflies' journey. Anderson suggested that they may fly more than 1,000 metres above the ground, where helpful winds could carry them towards the Maldives. But there was still one important question. Could their tiny bodies survive such a long flight? In 2021, an international team of researchers led by Johanna S U Hedlund studied how much energy these dragonflies would need to cross the ocean. Using computer models, they found that the insects could save enormous amounts of energy by gliding through the air and flapping their wings only when necessary. According to their calculations, a dragonfly using a combination of gliding and wing-flapping could potentially remain airborne for around 230 hours under favourable assumptions. By comparison, continuously flapping its wings would exhaust its estimated energy reserves in roughly four hours. The research showed why the right winds could make such an extraordinary crossing possible. However, these figures come from computer models. Scientists have yet to directly track individual globe skimmers throughout the proposed ocean journey. From India to Africa, but the same dragonfly doesn't make the whole trip The Maldives may be only one part of the story. In 2023, researchers from IIT Kharagpur, including Sanat Ranjan Kumar, Amit A Pawar, Arnab Roy and Sandeep Saha, examined how winds and rainfall could connect the dragonflies' movements across the Indian Ocean. Their research suggested a possible migration route: October to December: Dragonflies leave India and travel towards the Maldives as seasonal winds change. January to March: Favourable winds and rainfall may help them move towards the Seychelles and mainland Africa. May to July: Strong winds over the western Indian Ocean, known as the Somali Jet, may help later generations travel from Africa towards India. Some dragonflies may breed in temporary rainwater pools along the way, including on islands where suitable conditions exist. And here is an important detail. The dragonfly that leaves India is not necessarily the one that returns. The journey is believed to unfold across several generations. One generation travels, reproduces where conditions allow, and its offspring continue the movement. Researchers estimate that four to five generations may be involved over a year, with young dragonflies emerging approximately 45 to 60 days after breeding. The Wandering Glider (#Pantala flavescens), or Globe Skimmer, is a #dragonfly species known as the world's longest distance #insect traveller, aptly named based on its migrating behaviour. #AareyForest #aareycolony #Aarey #SGNP #Odonata #saveaareyforest #Biodiversity #Mumbai https://t.co/Txu3Z7PdU0 — Rajesh Sanap (@RajeshVS87) August 24, 2022 A remarkable journey that still holds mysteries Scientists have pieced together this possible migration by studying dragonfly sightings, rainfall, wind patterns and the energy needed for flight. While the arrival of globe skimmers in the Maldives is well documented, much of the proposed journey between India and Africa remains a scientific hypothesis supported by modelling and observations. There is still plenty to discover about the exact routes they take, where they breed and how they choose the winds that carry them. But the research already gives us a fascinating way to look at something as familiar as the monsoon. The same seasonal rains that fill our ponds, fields and lakes may also help make an extraordinary journey possible for an insect small enough to rest on our fingertip. And the next time you spot a dragonfly after the rains, consider this: a creature that looks so delicate may be capable of travelling farther than we could ever imagine. items.descriptionOriginal: Step off a busy Bengaluru road and into a tree-filled park, and the difference can be immediate. The harsh sun gives way to shade, and the air feels cooler. For a city once celebrated as India's Garden City, these green spaces have become especially valuable as concrete buildings and asphalt roads spread. But what if a park could help cool the streets around it, too? A 2026 study suggests that Bengaluru's parks are doing exactly that. Researchers found that their cooling influence can extend hundreds of metres beyond their boundaries. They also identified a surprising number that could help cities plan better parks: 2.49 hectares, or roughly six acres. How far can a park's cooling reach? Researchers Arpit Verma and Sonam Agrawal wanted to understand how Bengaluru's green spaces help reduce heat in the surrounding neighbourhoods. Their study, published in Advances in Space Research , examined 15 urban green spaces using satellite images collected during summer and winter. The findings were encouraging. Most parks showed a cooling effect of over 1 C in their immediate surroundings, even where buildings and roads covered more than 70% of the surrounding area. On average, this cooling extended approximately 186 to 246 metres beyond park boundaries, with stronger effects during summer. Think about what that could mean for a neighbourhood. A park's trees and vegetation may help reduce surface temperatures along nearby roads and built-up areas, benefiting spaces beyond those used by its visitors. Why trees make such a difference There is a simple reason parks tend to be cooler. Trees block sunlight from directly heating the ground. Plants also release moisture into the air, helping cool their surroundings. Concrete and asphalt behave differently. They absorb and retain heat, contributing to higher temperatures across heavily built-up neighbourhoods. This is part of what researchers call the urban heat island effect , where cities become hotter than their less-developed surroundings. Parks alone cannot resolve urban heat. Their effectiveness depends on vegetation, surrounding construction and the availability of space for green cover. Photograph: (News 18 Kannada) The Bengaluru study found that a park's ability to counter this heating depended on its size, shape and surrounding development. And that led researchers to an important question: How big should a park be to offer effective cooling? Why 2.49 hectares could be a useful benchmark The researchers discovered that bigger parks generally cooled a wider area. However, increasing their size did not always bring equally large improvements in cooling. Their calculations identified 2.49 hectares, approximately 6.15 acres, as an efficient size for cooling intensity, or how much a park reduces surrounding surface temperatures. For cooling a larger surrounding area, the suggested size was 5.29 hectares, or about 13 acres. These figures offer useful guidance for planners deciding how to use limited urban land. Bengaluru already has expansive green spaces such as Cubbon Park and Lalbagh. But residents across the city also need accessible greenery closer to their homes. The study suggests that thoughtfully planned neighbourhood parks could help, especially in areas crowded with buildings. What this means for Bengaluru's future There is one important distinction. The researchers measured land surface temperatures using satellites, rather than the air temperatures people experience. So, while the findings show how green spaces reduce surface heating, they cannot guarantee that every nearby street will feel a certain number of degrees cooler. The 2.49-hectare figure is also a planning benchmark, rather than a fixed rule for every park. BBMP is keen to reclaim Bengaluru's Garden City tag. Currently, 1408 parks gardens are being maintained by the civic body. While 1135 of them have been fully developed, work is on to beautify 273 #parks. #BBMP #Bengaluru https://t.co/LZuwUOEnXh — Maheshwar Rao.M, IAS (@GBAChiefComm) December 19, 2019 Still, the message for Bengaluru is valuable: protecting existing parks, planting trees and planning green spaces carefully can help tackle urban heat. For residents, a neighbourhood park is where children play, friends meet and people take their evening walks. The research shows that its benefits can travel beyond those familiar paths. And perhaps that is how Bengaluru can strengthen its Garden City identity: by ensuring that the greenery people enjoy inside a park can also help cool the neighbourhoods they call home. Sources: 'The interaction between urban heat island and urban parks: An in-situ measurement-based review' : By Semra Ogce, Huseyin Ogce, Siyu Yu, Robert D. Brown, Published on 31 May 2025 'Investigation of Urban Green Spaces as Potential Cooling Sources for Heat Mitigation in Bengaluru Metropolitan City, India' : By Arpit Verma and Sonam Agrawal, Published on 1 July 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe Reading Time: 3 minutes Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has helped saiga antelope rebound from about 20,000 to 4.6 million. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe has produced one of the largest wildlife recoveries on record. Saiga antelope numbers have climbed from roughly 20,000 in the early 2000s to about 4.6 million in 2026. The Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative has led this work since 2006. Altyn Dala means “golden steppe” in Kazakh. The initiative has helped protect 5 million hectares of grassland, an area larger than Denmark. It is also bringing back wild asses and wild horses that vanished from the region long ago. The saiga is a small antelope with a large, flexible nose that filters dust and warms cold air. Its herds migrate hundreds of miles across the steppe, a vast, dry grassland with few trees. By the early 2000s, those herds had nearly disappeared. After the Soviet Union collapsed, poaching surged across Central Asia. Hunters killed saigas for meat and for male horns, which sold for traditional medicine in Asia. Within about a decade, the population crashed by more than 95%. Five partners joined forces in 2006 to reverse that decline. Kazakhstan’s Committee for Forestry and Wildlife works with the Association for the Conservation of Biodiversity of Kazakhstan. Fauna & Flora, the Frankfurt Zoological Society, and the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds bring international support. Their first priority was stopping the killing. Ranger teams and aerial patrols now cover the saiga’s range. Sniffer dogs and customs training help catch horn smugglers at the border. Next, the partners needed to know where the herds went. Since 2009, researchers have fitted saigas with satellite tags to map their migrations. That data shows which areas need protection and when. New reserves followed the herds. The most recent, Bokey Orda-Ashiozek in western Kazakhstan, covers about 657,000 hectares. Wildlife corridors also link reserves through private land, under joint plans with landowners. The strategy faced its hardest test in 2015. During the spring calving season, more than 200,000 saigas died within weeks, over 60% of the global population. A 2018 study in Science Advances linked the deaths to a bacterium that turned deadly in hot, humid weather. Because poaching was under control, the surviving herds could rebuild. Aerial surveys each spring tracked the comeback. The 2024 count found about 2.8 million saigas, and the 2026 count reached roughly 4.6 million. That is about 230 times the low point. In December 2023, the IUCN Red List moved the saiga from Critically Endangered to Near Threatened. The Kazakh association’s director, Vera Voronova, called it one of the most successful land mammal recoveries ever recorded. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe means rebuilding the full community of grazing animals, not just one species. Kulan, a wild ass native to Central Asia, disappeared from the Torgai steppe more than 100 years ago. Scientists consider them a keystone species, since their grazing and movement help shape the grassland. Reintroductions began in 2017, and partners aim to establish about 100 kulan in the region. A recent group traveled 2,139 kilometers by road from Altyn-Emel National Park. After a year in an acclimatization pen, the animals went free in August 2025. Przewalski’s horses are following the same path. Considered the last truly wild horse species, they vanished from the wild by 1969 and survived only in zoos. In Kazakhstan, they had been gone for about 200 years. Przewalski’s horses returning to the wild are part of restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe after about 200 years. Photo by Wijs (Wise) on Pexels. The first seven horses arrived at the Altyn Dala reserve in 2024. More followed in 2025 from Prague Zoo and Hungary’s Hortobágy National Park. In May 2026, five of them left their pens and began roaming free. Officials plan to bring 40 to 45 horses by 2029, enough to sustain the herd. A stallion named Galvan wears a GPS collar so rangers can follow his movements. Local support makes these gains last. The initiative runs education programs in rural schools and has published children’s books about steppe wildlife in Kazakh. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe depends on the next generation valuing these animals. Recovery has also created new tensions. Farmers in several regions report that saigas damage crops and compete with livestock for pasture. Authorities are now studying how to manage herd sizes without undoing two decades of conservation. Roads, railways, and fences still break up migration routes. Wildfires and farm expansion put pressure on ground-nesting birds. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe will require balancing people and wildlife for years to come. Twenty years ago, the saiga seemed headed for extinction. Today, millions roam the plains, joined by wild asses and horses returning after a century or more. Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe shows what patient, well-coordinated protection can achieve. The post Saiga Comeback Leads the Way in Restoring Kazakhstan’s Golden Steppe appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: When Bridget Devaney's engagement ended after her fianc 's medical emergency, she was left holding plans for a trip to Northern Ireland and a wedding day that would never come. Rather than abandon it all, she posted an anonymous invitation on social media, and 11 women from the United States, Canada, and Wales said yes - to a stranger, a country, and an uncertain week. "When these women signed up for this trip, they didn't know my name. They didn't know what I looked like. They didn't know anything about me," Bridget told BBC News NI. On the day originally reserved for her wedding, the women dressed up and stood together against Northern Ireland's coastline for photographs that captured something the original plans never could have. What the trip quietly reveals is how much people are willing to show up for one another -- and how belonging can find us even in the ruins of what we thought our lives would look like.

items.descriptionOriginal: As winter approaches, the air across several Indian cities is likely to become harder to ignore. Smoggy mornings, hazy skies, and rising pollution levels often prompt families to rethink the air they breathe at home. Suddenly, an air purifier begins to look less like a luxury and more like a practical addition to the living room or bedroom. But walk into a store or browse online, and you will find air purifiers promising everything from cleaner air to near-total particle removal. One term appears repeatedly: HEPA. So, what does it actually mean? And how do you know whether the air purifier you are considering will do its job? Here are five things worth checking before you bring one home. 1. First, understand what HEPA means HEPA stands for High-Efficiency Particulate Air. In simple terms, it refers to a filter designed to trap tiny particles suspended in the air as it passes through the filter. According to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), a HEPA filter can theoretically remove at least 99.97% of airborne particles measuring 0.3 microns. To put that into perspective, a micron is one-millionth of a metre. These particles can include fine dust, pollen, mould spores and smoke particles. This makes HEPA filtration particularly useful when outdoor pollution finds its way indoors or when household dust and allergens become a concern . Choosing an air purifier with the right Clean Air Delivery Rate (CADR) can make a difference to how effectively it cleans the air in a room. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) However, not every product that mentions HEPA necessarily meets the same standard. Terms such as "HEPA-type" and "HEPA-like" do not, by themselves, establish that a filter meets a recognised HEPA performance specification. What to check: Look for a clearly stated filter grade and supporting performance information, rather than relying on the word HEPA alone. 2. Choose a purifier that suits your room Imagine buying a powerful air purifier for your bedroom, only to find that it struggles to clean the air in your larger living room. The problem may not be the filter itself, but the amount of air the machine can process. This is where CADR, or Clean Air Delivery Rate, comes in. It tells you how much filtered air a purifier delivers over a given period. A higher CADR generally means the machine can clean the air faster , provided the room size and other conditions are comparable. A purifier with a highly efficient filter may still be less effective in a large room if its airflow is insufficient. What to check: Match the manufacturer's recommended room size and CADR to the space where you plan to use the purifier. A bedroom and an open-plan living area may need different capacities. 3. Remember that HEPA filters do not remove everything HEPA filters are designed to capture particles, not every type of air pollutant. They do not, on their own, remove most gases, volatile organic compounds (VOCs) or odours. For instance, cooking can release particles into the air, while certain paints, cleaning products and new furniture can release gaseous chemicals. An activated-carbon filter can help adsorb some gases and odours. This is why some air purifiers combine HEPA filtration with activated carbon to tackle different kinds of indoor pollutants. While HEPA filters capture airborne particles, activated-carbon filters help tackle certain gases, chemicals and household odours. Photograph: ( Livemint ) What to check: If odours or gaseous pollutants are a concern, look for a purifier with an activated-carbon stage in addition to its particle filter. Check the manufacturer's specifications for what it is designed to remove. 4. Check the cost and availability of replacement filters Buying the machine is only the first expense. Filters collect particles over time and eventually need maintenance or replacement to keep the purifier working effectively. Replacement intervals vary depending on the model, how often it runs and the pollution levels in your surroundings. A filter used through a heavily polluted winter may need attention sooner than one used in cleaner conditions. What to check: Before purchasing, find out the price of a compatible replacement filter, whether it is readily available and how often the manufacturer recomm ends replacing it. Also check which parts can be cleaned and which must be replaced. 5. Look beyond the filter when comparing models A good filter is important, but the machine around it matters, too. Noise levels can affect whether you are comfortable running it at night, while energy consumption can influence your electricity bill if you use it for several hours each day. It is also worth checking the manufacturer's safety information. Some air-cleaning technologies, particularly ozone-generating devices, can introduce pollutants rather than simply remove them. Understanding how different filters work can help families make informed choices about improving indoor air quality. Photograph: ( MarketWatch ) What to check: Compare noise levels , power consumption, warranty, service support and safety specifications. Choose a model you can comfortably run and maintain as recommended. Cleaner air starts with informed choices As pollution levels rise, wanting to make the air at home a little cleaner is understandable. For families, it could mean being more mindful of the air children play in, the bedrooms where everyone sleeps, and the spaces where they spend most of their day. An air purifier can be one part of that effort. Taking a little time to understand the filter, choose the right model and maintain it well can help you make a more informed choice for your home. After all, cleaner indoor air begins with knowing what you are bringing through the door. Sources: 'What Is a HEPA Filter — and Does Filter Grade Actually Matter?' by Karban, Published on 11 April 2026. 'What is a HEPA filter?' by EPA. 'The HEPA Air Purifier: What You Need to Know!' by IQ Air, Published on 30 March 2017.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News American Red Wolf Pups Fostered into the Wild in North Carolina Reading Time: 3 minutes American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild bring fresh genes to a critically endangered species. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild mark a first in Saint Louis Zoo history. Three critically endangered, zoo-born pups now live with a wild Red Wolf family in North Carolina. Fewer than 40 American Red Wolves remain in the wild. They live only in northeastern North Carolina. That group would not even fill a single school bus. The wolves are critically endangered, which means they face a very high risk of extinction. Hunters nearly wiped them out in the 1800s and 1900s. They once roamed the southeastern United States and are native nowhere else. In the 1960s, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) teamed up with North American zoos. Together, they started a breeding and reintroduction program for the species. The three pups were born at the zoo’s Sears Lehmann, Jr. Wildlife Reserve. Staff collected them on April 20, when they were seven days old. They underwent a health exam before the trip. Zoo staff traveled with the pups to the Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge in northeast North Carolina. They cared for the pups hour by hour along the way. FWS biologists then placed them in a wild den, a shelter where a mother raises her young. Biologists watched the den to see whether the wild mother returned. She did, and she accepted the newcomers into her litter. Several months later, the pups began exploring outside the den, and trail cameras showed all three alive and thriving. This process is called fostering. A wild mother raises pups born elsewhere as part of her own litter. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild add new genes to a very small population. Genetic diversity helps a population stay healthy. It improves disease resistance and reduces the harm of inbreeding, which happens when close relatives breed. Timing is the biggest challenge. A foster must happen within the first 14 days of a pup’s life. That is when wolf mothers bond with their young and are most likely to accept new pups. Two groups share the work behind American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild. FWS monitors breeding among wild wolves. The Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) Saving Animals from Extinction (SAFE) Program guides breeding among wolves in zoos. When a wild litter is born, SAFE looks for zoo-born pups within that narrow window. In 2026, the Saint Louis Zoo’s litter was the only one born in professional care. Partnerships between zoos and wildlife biologists make American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild possible and bring new genes to a very small population. Photo courtesy of Saint Louis Zoo . Professional care means wolves living in zoos and similar facilities. These American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild were the only eligible pups in North America. Regina Mossotti leads the SAFE American Red Wolf Program and serves as the zoo’s vice president of animal care. She says every pup counts when fewer than 40 wolves remain. She sees fostering as a key way to give these pups a chance to support the species’ future. Emily Weller coordinates the FWS Red Wolf Recovery Program. She says several recovery actions rely on close teamwork with SAFE. The American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild show how zoo partnerships directly help wild wolves. The wild mother had a large litter. The zoo cross-fostered a few of her pups into its litter at the reserve. This swap helps ensure she can care well for each pup. The exchange also moves genes between wild wolves and zoo wolves. Experts call that a rare and valuable chance for species recovery. The reserve covers 355 acres, roughly 270 football fields, and is closed to visitors. Wolves there learn survival skills with minimal human contact, preparing them for a possible life in the wild. In 2021, the zoo announced plans to develop about 20 acres for wolf conservation. Today, the reserve holds seven habitats for breeding and conservation. The zoo will share photo and video updates on its social media pages and website. Federal biologists continue to support the wild population through the national red wolf recovery effort. Each of the American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild strengthens a population found in only one region. Other reintroduction projects show similar promise, such as efforts to return gray wolves in Colorado . Careful releases and strong partnerships can help wildlife recover. American Red Wolf pups fostered into the wild show what shared effort can achieve. Zoo staff, federal biologists, and a wild mother each played a role. items.titleOriginal: A Crane, a Duck & a Bird From the Arctic: What Happens When India's Wetlands Disappear?
items.description: Όταν η άνοδος του νερού απείλησε τη φωλιά ενός γερανού Sarus στο χωριό Madanpura στο ανατολικό Uttar Pradesh, δύο άνδρες μπήκαν μέσα. Ο τοπικός εθελοντής Chedi Kewat ειδοποίησε το Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) και συνεργάστηκε με τον βοηθό αγρού Ravindra Kumar Tripathi για να ασφαλίσει τη φωλιά χρησιμοποιώντας κοντάρια από μπαμπού. Τριάντα μία μέρες αργότερα, τα αυγά εκκολάπτονται. Ήταν μια μικρή διάσωση, bu…
items.descriptionOriginal: When rising water threatened a Sarus Crane's nest in Madanpura village in eastern Uttar Pradesh, two men stepped in. Local volunteer Chedi Kewat alerted the Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) and worked with field assistant Ravindra Kumar Tripathi to secure the nest using bamboo poles. Thirty-one days later, the eggs hatched. It was one small rescue, but it tells us something important about India's birds . Their survival can depend on the pond beside a village, the marsh near a farm or the muddy shoreline along a coast. And that is why a new national assessment of India's birds matters. On 19 October 2026, WTI announced that experts had begun assessing 1,211 bird species regularly found across India. More than 100 preliminary assessments had been opened for expert review. Among them, three wetland birds, the Sarus Crane, Marbled Duck and Grey Plover, offer a glimpse of what is at stake. Why a pond beside a farm could decide a crane's future The Sarus Crane, the world's tallest flying bird, often makes its home in flooded paddy fields, village ponds and shallow wetlands. During the monsoon, these places provide space to build nests and raise chicks. But when marshes are drained, pesticides threaten birds or power lines cross their habitat, their survival becomes harder. Wetlands must remain places where birds can feed, rest and breed. These same habitats can also help nearby communities by recharging groundwater and reducing the impact of floods. Photograph: (ICIMOD-India Water Portal) The Sarus Crane has been proposed as Vulnerable in India's new assessment, indicating a high risk of extinction in the wild nationally. Uttar Pradesh has an estimated 19,000-plus Sarus Cranes. Across 10 eastern districts, WTI works with farmers, local volunteers called Sarus Mitras and village committees to monitor nests and protect wetlands. These community efforts matter because many crane nesting sites lie beyond protected wildlife reserves. The duck with fewer places to spend winter Every winter, the Marbled Duck travels to India in search of shallow freshwater wetlands where aquatic plants provide food and shelter. It has been recorded in Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab and other states. But its proposed national conservation status is Endangered. Marshes are being drained, water bodies are changing and suitable habitats are disappearing across parts of its range. Because these ducks move between wetlands depending on water conditions , experts also need better monitoring to understand how their populations are changing. A bird that crosses continents, but faces a worrying decline The Grey Plover makes an extraordinary journey every winter, travelling from its Arctic breeding grounds to India's coastline. Here, it searches for food in coastal mudflats, where the retreating tide exposes small creatures. The exercise is being jointly undertaken by the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI), the IUCN SSC Centre for Species Survival India–Wildlife Trust of India (CSS India–WTI) and the State of India's Birds (SoIB) Photograph: (Chuck Homler, Focus On Wildlife) Its proposed national category is Least Concern. That sounds reassuring, but another assessment raises questions. The State of India's Birds 2025 update estimated a 78.99% decline in its long-term population trend in India. Globally, the species is classified as Vulnerable. This difference shows why experts must carefully examine population records and habitat changes before finalising a bird's conservation status. What protecting these birds really takes India's new assessment will examine where birds live, how many there are and whether their populations are changing. Birdwatchers' sightings and field research can help experts fill information gaps. But identifying a bird's risk is only one part of protecting it. Wetlands must remain places where birds can feed, rest and breed. These same habitats can also help nearby communities by recharging groundwater and reducing the impact of floods. For Arshad Hussain, who works with local communities through WTI's Sarus conservation project , some of the happiest moments come when a farmer calls to report a new nest or a hatched chick. In Madanpura, protecting one Sarus nest meant recognising the danger in time and acting together. Across India, that same care for everyday wetlands could give many more birds a better chance. Sources: 'India Launches Collaborative National Red List Assessment of 1,211 Bird Species' : By Wildlife Trust Of India, Published on 19 October 2026 'Transitioning Wintering Shorebirds to Agroecosystem: A Thorough Evaluation of Habitat Selection and Conservation Concern' : By Diversity-Biodiversity Conservation, Published on 29 December 2023 National Wetland Inventory and Assessment (NWIA) Atlas 'Mercury contamination: a hidden threat to long-distance migrant shorebirds in critical wintering sites on the west coast of India' : By K A Rubeena , K M Aarif, Published on 23 September 2025

items.descriptionOriginal: Turn on a tap to wash your hands. Notice how much water hits your palms, bounces off and disappears down the drain. Now imagine this happening hundreds of times a day across an office building, alongside hidden leaks and cooling systems that use millions of litres of water. How much of it is actually being used, and how much is simply going to waste? Chennai-based, IIT Madras-incubated startup EarthFokus is trying to answer that question. Founded in 2019 by Arun Subramanian and Rishi Vandan, the water-tech company helps commercial buildings monitor consumption, identify leaks, recover water lost through evaporation and reduce everyday usage. Its three solutions, WaterOS, EcoVapure and WaterFokus, tackle different parts of the problem. Together, the company says, they have helped over 130 commercial buildings save more than five billion litres of water. It began with a tap EarthFokus started with a small experiment. In 2019, Arun, an engineer, was approached by a neighbour who wanted to explore ways to reduce water consumption in their garden. Around the same time, Chennai was facing its Day Zero water crisis, when the city's reservoirs ran critically low. The crisis brought home the importance of conserving water, but Arun began by looking at something much more ordinary: a tap. A conventional tap can release around 10 to 12 litres of water per minute, says Rishi. Yet, while washing our hands, much of that water can bounce off our palms and flow away unused. The team developed a fixture that could bring the flow down to as little as 0.5 litres per minute. The idea was to use only as much water as the task required. The product attracted attention during the COVID-19 pandemic, when frequent handwashing became essential. EarthFokus also secured early orders from corporate clients, including Cognizant. What began as an experiment to reduce tap water flow grew into a water conservation startup incubated at IIT Madras. But the founders encountered an unexpected hurdle. Customers often viewed the fixture as just another plumbing accessory, rather than a solution that could reduce a building's water consumption. "We had to change that perspective," says Rishi. "I'm not a dealer or a trader who's pushing products to you. Rather, we're a solution provider who wants to enable reduction at your building." That realisation pushed EarthFokus beyond taps. Instead of simply selling water-saving products, the team began helping clients measure consumption and verify the savings their interventions delivered. Three ways buildings can stop wasting water As the startup worked with more buildings, it realised that inefficient taps were only one part of the problem. Hidden leaks, poor monitoring and water lost through cooling towers offered other opportunities for conservation. 1. WaterOS: Spotting leaks before they become bigger problems Think of WaterOS as a monitoring system for a building's water supply. The platform uses IoT-enabled flow meters and sensors installed at key points, including supply lines, floors, washrooms and cooling towers. These continuously collect data and send it to the cloud, giving facility managers a near-real-time picture of how water is being used. AI then helps identify unusual patterns. For instance, a restroom might typically see heavy water use during office hours and almost none overnight. If the system detects a steady flow at 2 am, it can flag the anomaly for investigation. The cause could be a running toilet or a leaking valve that might otherwise go unnoticed for weeks. Unlike a monthly water bill, which reveals consumption after the fact, this system helps teams identify potential problems sooner. WaterOS uses smart sensors and real-time monitoring to help commercial buildings detect leaks and track water consumption. The technical team explains that WaterOS learns normal consumption patterns based on factors such as time of day, occupancy and seasonal variation. It can then flag deviations for facility managers to investigate. This makes it easier to move from reacting to a problem after water has been wasted to identifying it earlier. 2. EcoVapure: Recovering water from cooling towers Some of the biggest water losses in commercial buildings happen where occupants rarely look. Cooling towers, used in offices, factories and data centres, remove heat by allowing water to evaporate. While this is an essential part of the cooling process, it also means water is continuously lost. Cooling towers also lose water when some is drained away (blowdown) or carried away as tiny droplets (drift), although evaporation is often the largest source. EarthFokus developed EcoVapure to recover some of that water. Its deployed technology, called Capture, is designed for cooling towers that produce a visible plume of water vapour. As the plume passes over a specially designed surface, droplets gather and grow until they fall back into the cooling system. The recovered water can also be collected separately for other uses. The company says the technology can recover roughly 30% of evaporation loss under relevant operating conditions, though the actual amount depends on the tower and its operating environment. EcoVapure captures water droplets from cooling tower plumes, helping buildings recover a portion of the water otherwise lost through evaporation. EarthFokus is also developing Convert, a second approach intended to recover water from cooling towers without visible plumes. For Rishi, the opportunity extends beyond individual buildings. Cooling towers are used across industries, including power generation and data centres, making water recovery a potential way to address losses in essential infrastructure. 3. WaterFokus: Saving water without changing habits WaterFokus focuses on reducing water use at the tap. Its fixtures and aerators control the flow of water while maintaining the feel of a strong stream. "Aerators do this by mixing air into the water as it exits the tap, while other low-flow fixtures use restrictors or specially designed nozzles," adds Siva T from the cooling towers tech team. The difference may be barely noticeable while washing your hands. But across hundreds or thousands of taps used repeatedly throughout the day, even small reductions can add up. The idea is to make conservation almost effortless : install the fixture, and less water is used without asking people to change their routines. WaterFokus aerators reduce water flow while maintaining a comfortable stream, helping save water without changing everyday habits. EarthFokus also manufactures its fixtures in metal, with durability in mind, rather than relying on plastic products that may need frequent replacement. Together, the three solutions address different aspects of water management: WaterOS helps buildings understand where water is going, EcoVapure recovers some of what is lost, and WaterFokus reduces consumption at the source. How tracking water helped a building spot wastage One of EarthFokus's clients is WeWork India, which previously relied on manual readings to track water consumption across its centres. The process was labour-intensive, and the data often arrived too late to help facility teams identify unusual patterns quickly. With IoT-based metering, WeWork now has a more continuous picture of its water use. "The biggest shift has been moving from estimated, manual figures to accurate, real-time data across every asset," says P. Seshashayan, Manager, Energy & Sustainability, WeWork India Management Ltd. According to the company, consumption fell from 45 litres per person per day to 29 litres. WeWork has set a target of reaching 20 litres per person per day by FY28. WeWork's team says real-time monitoring has also helped it identify unusual consumption patterns sooner and strengthen sustainability reporting. It is currently evaluating EarthFokus's aerators and considering water audits, but has not deployed EcoVapure. For Rishi, the impact becomes especially meaningful when he can put the numbers into perspective. EarthFokus combines smart monitoring, water recovery and low-flow fixtures to tackle water wastage across commercial buildings. "I've spent multiple interactions with clients visualising this five-billion-litre number," he says. He recalls thinking about how that volume could have helped cities facing water shortages, including Bengaluru during its recent water crisis. For him, the number represents both a milestone and an opportunity to do more. EarthFokus is exploring how cooling-tower recovery could add significantly to its savings as the technology scales. The company has also worked with IBM and Cognizant. Rishi recalls that introducing water-saving fixtures at Cognizant's Chennai operations helped cut daily water demand by nearly 80%, according to the company's account of the intervention. These experiences have reinforced an important lesson for the founders: measuring water use is only the beginning. The next step is to make changes, verify their impact and keep improving. How the startup plans to save even more water EarthFokus typically begins working with a building by assessing its water infrastructure and establishing a baseline for consumption. It then identifies potential reductions and introduces monitoring or other interventions, allowing facility teams to track progress. The approach also reflects a practical understanding of what encourages businesses to invest in conservation. Alongside environmental impact, solutions need to improve operational efficiency and deliver measurable results. From a single tap to more than 130 commercial buildings, EarthFokus's solutions have helped save over five billion litres of water. Looking ahead, EarthFokus wants to expand EcoVapure and develop a water-recovery technology that can be adopted in India and scaled internationally. For Rishi, however, the underlying problem remains simple. Whether it is a tap, a reverse-osmosis system or a cooling tower, we often use more water than we actually need. "The basic problem is that we end up using more than what we need because we take water for granted," he says. For him, conserving water begins with understanding where the water we already have is going and finding ways to prevent it from being wasted. All images courtesy of EarthFokus team

items.titleOriginal: Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST DAILY Εάν η σελίδα σας For You ήταν γεμάτη από άτομα που ακυρώνουν ραντεβού για μπότοξ επειδή άρχισαν να τρώνε περισσότερο σολομό, έχετε βρει την τάση "eat your skincare". Η υπόθεση είναι ότι η σωστή διατροφή μπορεί να κάνει αυτό που υπόσχεται ένα ντουλάπι φαρμάκων γεμάτο ορούς. Είναι, ειλικρινά, ελκυστικό… αλλά είναι επίσης μόνο εν μέρει tr…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If your For You Page has been full of people canceling Botox appointments because they started eating more salmon, you’ve found the “eat your skincare” trend. The premise is that the right diet can do what a medicine cabinet full of serums promises. It is, honestly, an appealing one… but it’s also only partly true. The route food takes to your skin When you eat, nutrients get absorbed in the GI tract and travel through the bloodstream to wherever your body decides to send them. There’s no targeting involved, so your skin gets what’s available once everything else takes its share. Topical skincare works on a different logic entirely, putting concentrated ingredients directly on one spot without the detour. “Wrinkles and collagen loss are multifactorial,” says Dr. Kseniya Kobets , Director of Cosmetic Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. “No single food or supplement is going to make a huge difference if the rest of your diet is poor, you are unhealthy or dealing with inflammation, excessive sun exposure or you don’t have a good skincare regimen.” Food can correct deficiencies that slow things down. Vitamin C and amino acids matter for collagen formation; fatty acids support the skin barrier. But more doesn’t mean more. “I think of it as filling the tank,” Dr. Kobets says. “You need the nutrients and building blocks, but overfilling it doesn’t make the collagen-making machinery work faster.” Too much vitamin C, she notes, can cause GI problems and, in some people, raise the risk of kidney stones. Can food protect you from the sun? Some of the content goes further: eat your sunscreen . That sounds ridiculous, but there’s real science underneath it. “There is interesting evidence around oral photoprotection ,” Dr. Kobets says. “Certain carotenoids, polyphenols and Polypodium leucotomos extract have been studied for increasing the skin’s resistance to UV-induced damage.” That’s not a reason to put the SPF away, though. “I sometimes think of these as an extra layer of defense, but definitely not an oral sunscreen,” she says. “No amount of blueberries, green tea or antioxidant supplements is going to replace properly applied and reapplied sunscreen, protective clothing and smart sun behavior.” What to eat for skin health If you want your diet to pull some weight here, the list is manageable. Dr. Sapna Palep , a dermatologist at Journelle Skin, recommends eggs, avocado, flaxseeds, walnuts, salmon, and dark chocolate, which between them cover protein, healthy fats, omega-3 fatty acids , and antioxidants. “Nutrition can influence inflammation, oxidative stress, the microbiome and skin-barrier function,” says Dr. Kobets. “What is good for your overall metabolic health tends to be good for your skin as well.” That’s the version of this trend that holds up: eating well really does support your skin, and the foods involved are things most of us would benefit from eating more of anyway. What food can’t do is replace sunscreen or stand in for a routine that’s doing something. Think of it as filling a role, not playing every position. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM History was made in governors’ races across the country on November 3. In ten states, voters chose candidates who had never held that office before as a matter of historical record, not just political preference: a Black woman elected to the governorship for the first time anywhere in the United States, the first Native American woman to lead any state, the first Latina governor of Texas, the first elected Latino governor of California, the first Black governors of Florida, Nevada, and Wisconsin, and the first women ever to win governor’s races in Tennessee, Minnesota, and Ohio. The wins came from both parties and from states that historically appeared to share very little common ground politically, which is part of what made the night so hard to categorize. Georgia elects the first Black woman governor in U.S. history The result that will end up in history books is from Georgia, where Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s race to become the first Black woman ever elected governor of any U.S. state. The country had never crossed this threshold before, not in 250 years of gubernatorial elections. Lance Bottoms is 56 and served as mayor of Atlanta from 2018 to 2022 before moving to Washington as an adviser to former President Joe Biden. Her defeat of Republican health care executive Rick Jackson also makes her the first Democrat to win a Georgia governor’s race in more than two decades, in a state that has been in political motion since it flipped in the 2020 presidential race. New Mexico’s Deb Haaland becomes the first Native American woman governor New Mexico voters sent Deb Haaland to the governor’s office, making her the first Native American woman to hold that position in any state. Haaland, who is of Pueblo Indian descent, has been making this kind of history for most of her public career. She was among the first Native American women elected to Congress, and later became the first Native American cabinet secretary when President Biden appointed her as Interior secretary. Her defeat of Republican Gregg Hull is one more memorable and significant accomplishment. Latino firsts in California and Texas California and Texas, the two most populous states in the country, will each have a Latino governor for the first time. In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra , who served as state attorney general before becoming Biden’s Health and Human Services secretary, defeated Republican Steve Hilton to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom. It was not a close race, but it crossed a threshold the state had never crossed despite having one of the largest Latino populations in the country. Texas is the bigger surprise. Democrat Gina Hinojosa , a state representative, defeated incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, one of the country’s most prominent conservative governors and a close ally of President Trump. Hinojosa is now both the first Latina governor of Texas and the first Democrat to hold the office in more than 30 years. Texas has been changing as its Latino population grows, and Tuesday’s result suggested that shift is now showing up at the top of the ballot. Florida, Nevada, and Wisconsin each elect their first Black governors Three more states elected their first Black governor on Tuesday, and these wins came from both sides of the aisle. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds, backed by President Trump, defeated Democrat David Jolly to succeed outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds has served in Congress since 2021 and spent two terms in the state legislature before that; he campaigned on affordability and pledged to continue Florida’s conservative direction. In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford , the state’s attorney general, defeated Republican incumbent Gov. Joe Lombardo to become the first Black governor of any state west of the Mississippi River. Ford had already been Nevada’s first Black Senate majority leader and its first Black attorney general; he first won a state legislature seat in 2012, after a career that included practicing law and teaching math. Wisconsin’s win went to Democrat David Crowley , a Milwaukee County executive who beat Republican Congressman Tom Tiffany despite being significantly outspent. His path to the general election is a saga in itself: Crowley suspended his primary campaign before rejoining the race, with the backing of outgoing Gov. Tony Evers, after the candidate he had been supporting dropped out. He ran as someone who can work across the aisle, and the result suggested Wisconsin voters believed him. Three more states elect their first women governors Three states that had never sent a woman to the governor’s office did so on Tuesday. In Tennessee, Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn won a race expected to favor her, though by a narrower margin than most anticipated. She focused on immigration, confronting China, and cutting spending, and will become the first woman ever to hold Tennessee’s governorship. In Minnesota, Democrat Amy Klobuchar defeated Republican Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House, and will become the state’s first woman governor when she takes office in January. Ohio produced the night’s biggest upset. Democrat Amy Acton , who served as the state’s chief public health officer during the pandemic, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a race that turned notably rough in its final weeks, with an attack ad against Acton drawing national attention and criticism. She is now Ohio’s first woman governor, its first Jewish governor, and the first Democrat to hold the office in 20 years. What ten firsts in one night adds up to These results don’t necessarily add up to a single story about where the country is heading. Rather, what each of them does share is that the voters who elected them have done something that hadn’t been done before. Whether that came from changing attitudes about representation, the particular strengths of individual candidates, or just the specific dynamics of this incredible moment in the history of the United States of America, an election night this concentrated in firsts is certainly one to be remembered. items.descriptionOriginal: A piglet saved from a potentially much unkinder fate is now living out the story of Babe after being taken in by a compassionate great-grandmother who owns an animal sanctuary in England. Retired veterinary nurse Carole Webb rescued the tiny fellow, dubbed Tom, after he was discovered on the side of the road in March at just 1 day old. It’s unclear how he came to be there, but Webb theorized that a sow may have given birth while being transported, and the piglet fell from the trailer. The person who found him kept him safe overnight before handing him over to her. FarmAnimalRescueSanctuary/SWNS Tom, who was about the size of a kitten at the time, was hand-reared indoors with hot water bottles and heat pads. Six months later, he’s grown into a pampered pig roaming a three-acre field at the Farm Animal Rescue Sanctuary in Stratford-upon-Avon. “Tom is really just like a real-life Babe,” Webb, 82, told SWNS, adding: “He’s really friendly with the chickens, he’s got a lot of chicken and cat friends — really anything that goes in to see him is his friend.” She said he acts more like a pet dog now than a typical pig, following the farm’s humans around and even coming when he’s called by name. He also has his own stuffed animals, loves to play, and enjoys his treats. “He plays around you and loves being near you. He’s got a big fluffy toy pig, and what he likes to do is lay over it,” she noted. “He loves his belly rubs, too — he’s just the friendliest little pig you could meet.” FarmAnimalRescueSanctuary/SWNS Named after Lord of the Rings character Tom Bombadil , Tom now weighs around 330-450 pounds, a big jump from the tiny piglet that could once fit in the palm of Webb’s hand. “He’s a bit boisterous so we don’t mix him with the sheep, but he’s got the run of one of the field,” said Webb. She noted that the sanctuary is home to about 350 animals, including sheep, cats, chickens, and one other pig. “We also feed the pigeons that are free-flying, and we’ve got an aviary that we put them in until they’re well,” she added. “We’ve got quite a collection.” The sanctuary is currently raising money to buy new land so it can continue caring for its animals. Donate here. This article was originally written by Adam Dutton for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets. items.descriptionOriginal: At the edge of India, one teacher is opening doors to a world of possibilities. Ashqar moved to Arunachal Pradesh through Sunbird Trust and began teaching at NSCBAV Karo in the remote Shi-Yomi district. What started as an opportunity to explore a part of India he knew little about soon became a much bigger commitment. Alongside teaching, he took on responsibilities in teacher training, community engagement, school activities and working closely with parents. Life in this remote region comes with challenges that many city schools rarely face. Poor roads, landslides, unreliable electricity and limited network connectivity make everyday tasks difficult. Medical facilities and essential shops can be several hours away. Yet, the children inspire Ashqar with their curiosity, talent and eagerness to learn. Now, he hopes to bring smartboards to the school and create at least one properly equipped smart classroom, giving these children access to visual and interactive learning resources. Because every child deserves the opportunity to learn, no matter how remote their home may be. Help Ashqar bring a smart classroom to these children. Share his story, spread the word and support his mission to make quality education accessible, even in India’s most remote communities. items.descriptionOriginal: Once the Diwali lights come down and the decorations are packed away , what happens to all those beautiful marigold garlands and rose petals? More often than not, they end up in the bin. But what if those same flowers could make your home smell wonderful, help your garden grow, or even give your old clothes a fresh splash of colour? Environmental consultant Thankam Kumaran believes there is plenty we can do with flowers long after the celebrations are over. Through her Instagram page @useful_human_being , she shares simple, creative ways to reduce everyday waste and make more sustainable choices. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Thankam Kumaran (@useful_human_being) In one of her videos, she shares seven ways to give leftover Diwali flowers a second life, using things you may already have at home. Give your festive flowers a second life 1. Make fragrant potpourri Collect the leftover flowers and place them in a small breathable bag. Add a few drops of essential oil and some camphor. Hang the bag in a room to release a pleasant fragrance and keep the space smelling fresh. 2. Prepare bio-enzymes Use the leftover flowers to make bio-enzymes through fermentation. This gives discarded floral waste another purpose instead of sending it to the bin. 3. Make incense sticks Dried flowers can be repurposed to make homemade incense sticks, allowing you to put the petals to use even after the celebrations. 4. Dye fabrics naturally Flower petals can also be used to extract natural colours and experiment with dyeing clothes and other fabrics. 5. Make homemade shampoo Certain flowers can be used to prepare homemade shampoo, offering another way to make use of what would otherwise be discarded. Environmental consultant Thankam Kumaran shares seven ways to reuse puja flowers. Photograph: (Orissa POST) 6. Turn them into compost Add leftover flowers to your compost pile. As they break down, they contribute organic matter that can help nourish the soil in your garden. 7. Use them as mulch Dried flowers can be spread around the base of plants as mulch. This helps cover the soil and retain moisture while making use of festive leftovers. Instead of treating flowers as waste once Diwali is over, these ideas provide easy ways to extend their usefulness. Whether you turn them into something fragrant for your home or use them to nourish your garden, a little effort can keep festive flowers from going to waste.

Ο συγγραφέας Rajeev Balasubramanyam παρακολούθησε τη θλίψη στο δωμάτιο να θάβεται υπό απόσπαση της προσοχής και αποφάσισε κάτι…
items.descriptionOriginal: At a funeral for a man who never told anyone he was unhappy, the surviving friends sat around a table and talked about computer games. That detail -- precise and painful -- is where this essay begins, and it sets up everything that follows. Writer Rajeev Balasubramanyam watched the grief in the room get buried under distraction and decided something had to change. He called three old friends scattered across Vancouver, London, Brussels, and Berlin, and he proposed the thing none of them had ever done: a men's circle. The rules were simple -- take turns speaking while others listen and no advice-giving. That last rule proved harder than it sounds; as he notes, dispensing solutions is simply "the way that we, as men, were used to talking." What emerged instead was something quieter and more rare: the feeling of being held. Over a year of online circles, a father died, a cancer survivor admitted he wasn't as fine as he'd thought, and a man in grief finally had space to feel it.
