items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank and happened to touch, and within days the bleached one started absorbing healthy algae directly through the contact point with its neighbor. The researchers hadn’t designed that experiment, which is part of what makes the discovery so striking: a potential recovery mechanism for bleached coral hiding in plain sight, requiring nothing more than the right genetic match and direct physical contact. Arielle and Karissa cover ten solutions this week, including a brain therapy reporting 68 percent remission for PTSD when decades of medication have only reached 11, a wildlife sanctuary in Austin that runs on Twitch donations and reaches the conservation audience that broadcast nature documentaries never could, and the solar panels now legal for California renters that require no contractor, no roof, and no tens of thousands of dollars upfront. If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Intro Arielle: Hello, it’s Arielle. Karissa: And I’m Karissa. Arielle: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup. How are you, Karissa? Karissa: Um, feeling pretty tired. Trying to adjust to the time change here, so. Arielle: Oh, yeah. You guys had your time change in the States this past weekend, right? Karissa: Mm-hmm. Yeah, and I know you had it the weekend before. But yeah, this week has been, been all about adjustment. Arielle: It’s a bit of a transition period. I feel like a lot of my friends are going through transitions right now, and it kind of aligns with the seasons. And also Thanksgiving is coming up. Well, I mean, Canadian Thanksgiving already happened in October, and that’s what I grew up with. But you guys have your Thanksgiving soon. And, uh, to celebrate, we’re doing our local changemaker series like we do every year. Karissa: Yeah, it’s always one of our favorite times of year, too, to give back to The Optimist Daily community and report on the changemakers that are making a difference in your lives and your communities. Speaking of gratitude, we’re very grateful for all of you Optimists who keep The Optimist Daily going in our shared resolve to get positive news out there. And we also wanna thank our Emissaries, who are the financial supporters of The Optimist Daily. Arielle: We have big love for our Emissaries. They help us keep the lights on here. But there are a lot of free ways that you can help support this mission as well, ’cause we know that not everybody has the budget to donate, and that’s completely fine. But if you wanted to help our cause in other ways, you can follow us on socials. We are @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism. And along with that, you can share our content on your own personal stories or send them directly to friends and family who you think need a little bit more positivity in their lives. All of that helps us out a lot. Karissa: You can also email us at podcast@optimistdaily.com, or reach out to us on any of the platforms we’re on. Arielle: All right. Well, with all of that said and done, I think I’m going to jump into this week’s solutions. Sardinian restaurants banning phones Arielle: The first one is titled “Sardinian restaurants are banning phones for families at meals”. So in Sardinia, 15 restaurants are asking families to put their phones away when they sit down to eat. In exchange, staff hand them a box of games designed by pediatricians to help parents and kids actually talk to each other. Do you find yourself either seeing people out at a restaurant who aren’t actually engaging with each other ’cause they’re on their phones, or do you find yourself doing that as well, Karissa? Karissa: I mean, I definitely see people doing it, and I try my hardest not to do it. Usually when I’m out at dinner it’s with someone maybe I haven’t seen in a while, so we have lots to talk about, so really try not to. But I, I mean, I can be guilty sometimes if I’m just out at dinner, um, with maybe my family or my boyfriend because, you know, we’re talking all the time, so I’m like, “Well, let me just pull it out for a second while we’re waiting.” Arielle: Yeah, I try my best to just keep my phone, um, where I can’t see it when I’m with other people. Yeah. But I… If I’m eating by myself then I will- Karissa: Mm. Arielle: … um, distract myself with my phone, you know? What I like about this screen time story is that it’s a little bit different from the typical one that you see. It’s not, like, just a lecture or, or, like, a rule. There’s actually a- Yeah … kit. It’s a pediatrician-designed game box that the restaurant itself will hand you so that you have something in your hands other than a phone. So that to me is, like, a structural solution and not so much of a moral one. Or it is, but, like, there’s more structure to it. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Anna Cau, she’s the Children’s Ombudsman, which is an independent official appointed to receive, investigate, and help resolve complaints made by individuals against government agencies, public authorities, or private organizations, if you didn’t know. That I got from Wikipedia. But she’s the woman who designed the scheme, and she makes this point: Most screen time debates put the whole problem on parents, and she’s saying the spaces families move through, like restaurants and anywhere in public life, they should also be part of the solution. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: And this is based in Sardinia, uh, which is in Italy. And there, the communal meal carries a lot of cultural weight. Yeah. I mean, it carries weight everywhere because eating is such a social human practice. But in Italy especially, if the- Karissa: Yeah … Arielle: dinner table is losing to screens over there, then that’s a, a real signal. So yeah, I just really enjoyed reading about this solution, and maybe it will inspire other people who are listening to have their own kind of phone-free dinners. And, uh, you know, I’m sure you can look up engaging questions online or create your own questions to ask your family members as well. You don’t need to have this, uh, specific game box or pediatrician-designed kit. California balcony solar for renters Arielle: The next solution is titled “California legalizes balcony solar for renters and beyond”. We’ve been hearing a lot about solar energy and apartment dwellers being able to participate in that, but this is quite local to you, Karissa, ’cause California just legalized plug-in solar panels, and for the first time, that includes renters. Panels that cost a few hundred dollars that you hang off your balcony or stick outside a window that could cut your electricity bill by up to $500 a year are now legal. So there’s no contractor, no roof, no tens of thousands of dollars upfront for Californians who live in apartments. California is the 10th state to pass this kind of law. It’s the biggest electricity market in the country, so when California moves, then manufacturers basically have to follow. The goal advocates keep describing is plug-in solar on a shelf at a hardware store like any other appliance, and that’s finally a realistic near-term thing. First green star discovered Arielle: The next solution is a pretty fun one. It’s titled “Astronomers discovered first green star ever, and it’s powered by a dead planet’s chemistry”. Astronomers just found the first green star ever documented, a white dwarf that glows chartreuse, not because of temperature, but because it absorbed sodium from a planetary system it destroyed. A star that ate its planets and turned green. It’s like a sci-fi. I was just- Yeah … fascinated by this whole solution. We’ve always assumed star colors track with temperature, like iron heating in a blacksmith’s forge, if you can imagine, like, it goes from red to white hot, and this star kind of broke that model. Its color is a chemical record of what it’s consumed. Carbon-rich atmospheres glow pink or purple. Stars that absorbed asteroid or planetary material go yellow. But then this one went green. There’s a lot more on the science within the article itself. Uh, but yeah, I just found the whole thing quite interesting. I just think it’s really cool to think about all of this unexpected, completely surprising stuff happening in this universe. Great Koala National Park Arielle: Okay, moving on to the next solution, which is titled, “How carbon credits helped unlock the Great Koala National Park in New South Wales, Australia.” After more than a decade of campaigning, three state elections, and 14 hours of parliamentary debate, Australia’s Great Koala National Park is officially real. It’s 478,000 hectares of protected habitat, which is roughly 1.2 million acres, and the thing that finally made it financially viable was carbon credits. The part about carbon credits is what makes the economics work. The government registered over 117,000 hectares of the park state forests with the Federal Clean Energy Regulator. By ending native forest logging there, they can now sell carbon credits from the land. Protected forest generates more revenue than logged timber, it turns out, and that’s the financial argument that helped get this through. The article goes into the human cost. It didn’t wanna glaze over that detail. The forestry corporation already cut 30-plus jobs in Coffs Harbour before the park was even finalized, and then there’s also timber suppliers and trucking companies, engineering firms, all of these places of employment that have to let a lot of people go. So the government- Yeah … is committed to moving displaced workers into national parks roles, but that transition is still underway, and I’m sure it will go through some growing pains. Ashley Love, the conservationist who started this campaign after locals told him koalas weren’t as common as they used to be, called the result, “Quite fragmented with connectivity gaps still to close.” But he’s already pushing for the sections that didn’t make it into the park. And yeah, after a decade, he sounds less frustrated than just persistent, because this is still such an accomplishment. Karissa: Conservation campaigns that connect land protection to economic logic are always gonna be more viable. I think it’s a good model to follow, and, um, just a, a win for the koalas. Arielle: Mm-hmm. It’s a win for the koalas, and a win for Australia’s broader biodiversity as a whole. Coral healing through touch Arielle: The last solution that I’m going to share with everyone before I hand over the reins to Karissa is “Stanford scientists discovered bleached coral can heal through touch”. Two coral fragments accidentally fell over and touched each other in a Stanford lab tank. Within days, the fragment that was bleached started recovering, absorbing healthy algae directly through the point of contact with the healthy coral fragment. The researchers were blown away because this was not supposed to happen. It was not really their experiment at all. What makes it scientifically interesting is how specific the conditions have to be for this to happen. It only works with direct physical contact and only between genetically identical corals. If you separate them by a few millimeters, then nothing will happen. If you introduce a different genetic background, then they reject each other, much like a mismatched organ transplant. Genetic twins in contact create what the team calls a tissue bridge, which is a nutrient highway between them The IUCN announced that about 96% of the world’s shallow water reef systems are critically endangered and could disappear by 2075. Coral reefs support between a quarter and a third of all marine species, so this discovery is a glimmer of hope in a very dark picture. Maya Higa’s wildlife sanctuary on Twitch Karissa: Okay, so this is one of our local Change Makers series articles, and it’s about Maya Higa, who built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch funded by the people who watch it. Earlier this year, Maya was on a trip to Dominica and was offered the chance to swim with sperm whales, and she said no. Her followers couldn’t be there, and that one decision pretty much captures what she built Alveus Sanctuary to do and explains how a Twitch stream became a $7.5 million conservation platform. Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin and a virtual conservation classroom. Animal ambassadors, animals that can’t survive in the wild, live at the sanctuary, while a 24/7 live stream lets viewers watch, learn, and get to know individual animals by name. And Maya’s background isn’t just as a creator. She’s a former zookeeper with a falconry license and a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. So all that knowledge is what this stream runs on. The demographic she’s reaching is one that traditional conservation has struggled to reach for decades. She’s reaching 18 to 30-year-olds through social media in ways that broadcast nature documentaries never could. Arielle: Yeah, it’s such a smart move. You know, a lot of the time the depiction of the younger generation is that their attention spans are really, um, short, which in some ways is true, but there’s also a lot of young people who just love to watch streams, and those are like- Yeah … long-form, like the longest form content there is. So yeah, really big shout-out to Maya. This is an incredible project. And yeah, I, I think I’m gonna start watching … the animals as well. Karissa: I love this whole idea, and of course they’re targeting the younger viewers, but I think it kind of reaches across the ages as well. Um, my mind goes to in California, Jackie and Shadow, the bald eagles that- Yeah lived in Big Bear Lake, I think captured the hearts of many. So once again, congrats to Maya, and check out the article for more details. Solar kits for disaster relief Karissa: The next solution is “Solar kits are changing what disaster relief looks like”. Every morning in a refugee camp in Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo and tarpaulin shelter and puts out a solar panel. He’s done it for six years since his family fled the Rohingya crackdown in Myanmar. That one panel is how his whole family charges phones, cooks with light, and keeps fans running through the heat. And this story is about what this technology is actually for. The range of where this is happening right now is pretty striking. Doctors Without Borders is running a tuberculosis clinic on solar in Karachi, and UN water filtration on solar in South Sudan. And kits were distributed after Nepal’s floods that killed over 1,400 people. And a nonprofit in Ukraine has given kits to thousands of families, including 75 and 80-year-old grandparents who just plug them in. The CEO said, “It’s just a matter of plug and play for these solar relief kits.” And I mean, that goes back to our earlier solution of the plug-in balcony solar panels. But switching from diesel to solar is harder than it sounds for aid organizations because long-running generator contracts are still going on. There’s new distribution chains that have to be navigated in genuinely dangerous conditions. In addition, recent donor funding cuts have made it harder to transition to new technology. So one program leader said flat out, “Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut.” Arielle: Yeah, it’s interesting. Whenever I think about solar panels, I think about the types of solutions that we’ve been hearing about so far, like the rooftop solar in Australia for apartments or the plug-in solar or solar panels above farm fields. But I don’t really think about it in this context where it could be so, so useful for disaster relief or- Yeah for places that don’t have access to a reliable grid. Uh, so I think it’s really encouraging that this technology is reaching all corners of the world for all types of contexts and situations. Household uses for toothpaste Karissa: The next story is a lifestyle solution, and it’s “Eight surprising household uses for toothpaste from a pro cleaner”. So there’s probably a tube of toothpaste in your bathroom right now, and if it’s only going on your teeth, you’re leaving a surprisingly useful cleaning tool just sitting in the drawer. A professional cleaner shared the eight household jobs she regularly uses it for, and some of them are actually not that obvious. Plain, white, non-gel toothpaste has mild abrasive particles that work like an ultra-fine sandpaper, and that’s why it can buff out light scratches on glass, phone screens, and wood surfaces, and polish metal fixtures, so lots of different uses. Gel toothpaste doesn’t have those particles, so it doesn’t work the same way, and that’s just something to keep in mind when you reach for that toothpaste. One use I was surprised to read is using toothpaste for a fogged car headlight, and it’s one that a lot of people haven’t heard, and it’s really simple. You just rub toothpaste over the lens in small circles for about a minute or two, rinse, dry, and repeat if needed. So no specialty product is required to clear up those fogged headlights. There’s just kind of this huge appetite right now, especially with the economy and the whole idea of sustainability as well, to, you know, use things you already own and get creative with them. It’s practical, it’s low cost, and it’s also satisfying as well. Brain therapy for PTSD Karissa: Moving on to the next solution, “Personalized brain therapy hits 68% remission for PTSD”. The best FDA-approved medications for PTSD have a remission rate of about 11%. But a newly FDA-cleared brain therapy just reported a 68% remission, and that’s not a typo. That is a big difference. It’s the first non-drug treatment specifically cleared for PTSD since the diagnosis was formally recognized in 1980. How this therapy works is that you get an EEG that maps your specific brain electrical activity, and an AI algorithm builds a personalized stimulation plan from that data. Then a coil placed against your scalp delivers targeted magnetic pulses, and you do this for five sessions a week for five to six weeks. The lead researcher described standard brain stimulation as covering the leak with a tarp, and this treatment tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. This is important for many different populations because about 6% of Americans will experience PTSD in their lifetime with higher rates among women and veterans. Approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day in the US. The two SSRIs approved for PTSD have been the only FDA-approved options since 1980, and 11% remission means the vast majority haven’t gotten there on medications alone. So this is a really great breakthrough, and of course, accessibility is going to be the next hurdle. Um, you know, teams are actively trying to work on getting this covered by insurance, and FDA clearance is not the same as accessibility, so this gap is the next fight Volunteering this Thanksgiving Karissa: The final solution I have to share is “The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving, 17 options for every schedule”. Every year around Thanksgiving, a lot of people have the same thought, “This is the year I actually do something.” And then they show up at a food bank and find out every other person in town had the same idea. There’s actually a smarter way to do this, and several options that don’t even require leaving your couch at all. So I think the most important point out of this article, even though it gives tips to volunteer and help around, is that holiday demand often creates more volunteers than organizations can actually use on Thanksgiving Day itself. And a lot of that is directed at food banks. So if you want your time to count, definitely call ahead and see if you’re needed. And if you get redirected because a location is at capacity, ask when they need people the most. The answer is almost always in February, when the holiday energy has faded out, but the need hasn’t. And I think that’s just a really good point. These organizations need your help year-round, and that’s important to keep in mind. So this list covers every kind of situation, whether it’s Feeding America, Meals on Wheels, and Operation Turkey, and about the tightly organized shifts they have. But it also covers options that are remote, like writing letters to deployed service members through Support Our Troops, and animal shelters for people who are better with dogs than crowds. So lots of ways to volunteer this giving, thankful, grateful season. So yeah, I think it’s just a great reminder, and hard to believe that Thanksgiving is already around the corner. Arielle: Yeah, I totally agree. I, I didn’t really think too much about the oversaturation in the volunteering space for the holiday season. It does make sense, though. So, you know, I, I think if you’re interested in volunteering and just haven’t gotten around to it yet, then maybe the holiday season is a great place to start. But then it could be your gateway into doing it- Karissa: Yeah … Arielle: more regularly as well. Outro & quote Karissa: Well, that’s all of the positive news we had to share this week on The Optimist Daily. But before we go, we’ll leave you off with a quote. ” Arielle: Having a good time together is the essence of lovingness and the best means of increasing it.” That’s from Benjamin Spock, and I think that’s a great quote to go with quite a few of our stories today. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. That’s why I wanted to include it in today’s, uh, roundup. Arielle: We will be back next week with more solutions. In the meantime, Karissa and I wish all of you Optimists and Emissaries a wonderful weekend. Karissa: Yeah. Bye, everyone. Arielle: Bye. The post Podcast Transcript November 6th, 2026— 2 coral fragments touched in a Stanford lab: a story of healing (plus 9 more solutions) first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Solar panels above, fish below: That’s the idea behind aquavoltaics, an emerging way to pair solar power with fish farming. Freshwater aquaculture produces more than 160 million tons of fish, crabs, and shrimp a year, emitting an estimated 438 million tons of CO 2 equivalents (tCO 2 eq). A new study finds that covering the world’s aquaculture ponds with floating solar panels could generate nearly as much electricity as the United States uses, far more than enough to offset the industry’s carbon footprint. Photovoltaic electricity is Earth’s most abundant potential source of renewable energy, but it requires lots of surface area. So people have tried to combine it with other types of land use, spawning agrivoltaics , in which solar panels are spaced across farm fields or pastures —harvesting a fraction of the incoming sunlight without appreciably reducing crop yields. People have also tried covering lakes , canals, and reservoirs with photovoltaic panels —but the wildly fluctuating levels and large size of these water bodies present major challenges. Aquaculture ponds , in contrast, are generally small and shallow, with consistent water levels. In the new study, the authors analyzed satellite imagery and other data to estimate the total global area of aquaculture ponds. They identified 50,000 square km of these ponds worldwide, of which only 423 square km currently host water-surface photovoltaics. Some 97 percent of this aquavoltaic area was in China, with most of the rest in Vietnam, South Korea, Thailand, and Israel. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area The authors estimated that the electricity generated (4,100 TWhr/yr) could replace enough fossil fuel-derived energy to avoid 2.5 billion tCO 2 eq per year—nearly six times the current emissions of aquaculture worldwide. This electricity production would concentrate along the coastlines of South and East Asia (including Indonesia and the Philippines), with additional hotspots in coastal regions of the Middle East, Egypt, Southern Europe, Central America, Mexico, South America, and the U.S. This locally produced power could cover the current national electricity needs of Vietnam, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Myanmar, the Philippines, Cambodia, Ecuador, Honduras, and Nicaragua. This aquavoltaic energy would be produced in non-industrial regions that are often not well connected to larger power grids—potentially sustaining over 800 small- and medium-sized cities worldwide. These calculations rest on baselines that will need to be refined for different regions, fish and crustacean species—including the assumption that 40 percent coverage of the water surface won’t compromise aquaculture yields. But it raises the possibility that aquavoltaics—a sector that didn’t even exist prior to 2010—could help drive our transition to renewable energy. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Many Ways Student-Led Climate Action Can Look Reading Time: 3 minutes Three Canadian schools doing three completely different projects, all with one common thread. By now, we can see that climate action doesn’t take just one shape. There are so many climate solutions that exist in this world, and it is particularly through the creativity and audacity of youth that we can implement them in the epicentres of community: schools. Sometimes, it’s a bike event that nearly 200 people show up to, or a compost bin that accidentally became a garden over summer break, or a dusty shed that a shop class turned into a net-zero community hub. Across three schools in the Canadian provinces of Newfoundland & Labrador, Ontario, and Prince Edward Island, students have been building, growing, and pedalling their way toward a greener school and pulling their communities along for the ride. Most students at École St. Matthew’s in St. John’s, Newfoundland live within two kilometres of their school, yet most arrive by car anyway. The school set out to change that habit with its annual spring community event: Bikefest. Their annual community cycling Bikefest, held in May, drew 164 registered participants (double last year’s 82), plus walk-ins that pushed the total close to 200. Their local Member of Parliament and the provincial Minister of Education both attended, and 15 children were matched with refurbished bikes and scooters and given helmets through a re-CYCLING initiative the school plans to expand next year. Additionally, one of Canada’s most prominent youth climate action journals, The Starfish Canada , even interviewed and published a piece on the project a few months later. Behind the event is a longer project that has installed bike racks, a repair station, and solar lighting at the school, while hosting safety courses and family cycling days. Student lead Sawyer wrote letters to local businesses asking for helmet discounts and volunteer support, and he received more responses than the emails his teacher sent. The city is starting to notice, too! “The city’s starting to see that shared use pathways are an opportunity,” said teacher lead Mr. Shoemaker. “We can get people walking. We can get people more healthy.” This next project started during lockdown, when a group of friends attending Eden High School in Ontario discovered they liked plants. When school returned in person, they formed a greenhouse club, only to find their school’s greenhouse had sat unused for decades, overtaken by overgrown plants and falling into disrepair. They cleared it out, researched how to repair it, and got to work. A student at Eden High School tends to their plants in their school’s greenhouse. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . The greenhouse is now fully functional, sealed against winter heat loss and actively used by students learning sustainable agriculture. A composting program ran successfully alongside it until the compost bin spontaneously became a volunteer garden over the summer, which is honestly a great problem to have. More recently, the school received a Go Wild grant from WWF Canada to build a wildflower pollinator garden beside the greenhouse. What began as a club fixing a broken structure has grown into a broader ecological vision for the school. “In a way, this project has launched our school into somewhat of a larger eco project,” said teacher lead Mike Idzenga. A Grade 9 student put it simply: “With all the tips and tricks that I learned this year, for the rest of my life I can do that to plant my own garden.” Three Oaks High School doesn’t shy away from hosting events: sports games, races, community presentations. When they finally built a new outdoor sports field, it came with an awkward problem: it was far from the kitchen where food for events was prepared. The TOSH Cares Club and shop program decided to fix it by using the unused shed sitting on school property. Students gather at Three Oaks High School to retrofit their multipurpose outbuilding. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . Students across programs retrofitted the building, insulating it, wiring a solar system, and turning it into a net-zero multipurpose outbuilding that can now host classes, clubs, and events. Many TOSH Cares students had never taken shop before, and many shop students had never engaged with environmental education. The project brought them together, and both groups left changed. A sign on the shed now describes its net-zero impact to anyone who walks by. Gabby Cierra, a Grade 12 student, said something worth sitting with: “It kinda feels like we almost can’t make as much of an impact because we are not old enough to start big programs… but I think this is an example that we can.” All three of these schools came to N:OW for Net-Zero , a pan-Canadian student-led climate action program, with a real, tangible wish to improve their school grounds and, ultimately, enhance the living conditions of those attending and surrounding them. If this isn’t proof that climate action looks like whatever young people decide to make it, then we don’t know what is! The post The Many Ways Student-Led Climate Action Can Look appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to The Spark, our monthly celebration of how people just like you are creating positive change, one meaningful step at a time. The Spark is generously supported by Laura Rice. Sign up to Reasons to be Cheerful’s weekly newsletter here and you’ll get The Spark in your inbox at the start of each month. In this issue The power of community land trusts Cool roofs, cooler homes The perks of intergenerational roommates A community takes back its land In 2019, Nachand Trabue began noticing investors’ “We buy houses” signs all over her corner of Louisville, Kentucky. A historically Black neighborhood since the Civil War, Smoketown has deep roots and a long, proud past — including the city’s first Black library and first Black dentist, and as the birthplace of Muhammed Ali. But increasingly, long-term residents were getting priced out of their own community. For those like Trabue, a fourth-generation resident who remembered Smoketown in its thriving heyday, the change in their community was especially galling. “Because they’re taking away everything that made Smoketown great. They’re buying up the parks, the vacant lots, and putting in houses. There’s nothing for the kids. There’s no enrichment, no activity,” says Theresa Boyd, executive director of Smoketown Community Land Trust. A mural in Smoketown by The Art of Kacy. Credit: Don Sniegowski Trabue had had enough — she started pulling out the investors’ signs, reached out to the city’s land bank to figure out which vacant lots in the neighborhood were held by the city and connected with River City Housing , a local nonprofit home developer, to see how they could work together. At the same time, “the Smoketown Originals started to come together,” says Boyd, referring to a community organization of older residents with deep roots in the neighborhood. “They went to the churches, the community centers, the youth centers.” They started pushing the city to do a housing needs assessment and got in touch with Grounded Solutions , a national nonprofit for affordable housing, to decide whether a community land trust would be a viable option. Community land trusts (CLTs) are grassroots nonprofits that provide long-term affordable housing by buying and developing land on behalf of the community. When selling or renting homes, the CLT retains ownership of the land they’re built on, which makes the homes cheaper and keeps the land itself under community control. Crucially, CLTs also preserve affordability long-term by requiring owners to sell at an affordable price. The first CLTs grew out of the civil rights movement to secure land ownership for Black farmers. Today, they are an increasingly popular way of protecting land from speculators and creating long-term affordable housing, with over 300 CLTs in the US . The CLT’s first houses were recently completed, and more plots have already been chosen. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT In Smoketown, a lot of the initial work focused on explaining what a CLT is and getting the broader community on board. “Communities that have been divested [from] and have been talked to and at versus with, they lose their voice,” says Boyd. “We really had to rally the troops here in the community to be like, ‘You actually have a say in what goes on in your community.’” In 2020 the community and its partner organizations won the city’s Request for Proposals, securing $2.1 million to create a CLT. By 2023 the CLT was formalized and Boyd was brought onboard as the executive director. “I really whipped us into shape administratively and organizationally,” she says. “But most importantly, I went back out into the community and I was like, ‘Okay, this is what you wanted. Now what are we going to do with this land?’” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Based on a series of surveys, Smoketown CLT built its first seven houses right across the street from where Muhammed Ali threw his first punches under the watchful eye of trainer Fred Stoner, the grandfather of the CLT board president. These houses were recently completed, and the next seven plots have already been chosen. Before starting new developments, the CLT approaches the people living around the plots, says Boyd. “We invite them to the table: Okay, what are your concerns? What are your comments? This is what we are thinking. Is it a viable housing option for your street?” CLTs come in many different shapes, sizes and funding arrangements. In Smoketown, the CLT is funding the construction of the houses, but received the plots of land for free from the city. The land bank has earmarked around 70 plots in the neighborhood for the trust, says Boyd: “We were fortunate that those that came before me had enough gall to go to the city and be like, “Y’all holding all this land and you are absolutely not going to give it to investors. You are going to earmark it for the Community Land Trust.’ And we made them put it in writing.” Mayor Craig Greenberg joined Smoketown CLT to celebrate the completion of the CLT’s first seven homes. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT The city government has been supportive of the CLT, says Boyd, but it would not have happened without the community putting years of work into it. “Louisville’s been around for a really long time, and the people in our community absolutely will hold them to task, and that’s absolutely what they did. They started showing up at the council meetings, the reallocation of funds.” Partnering with experts, like Grounded Solutions, is key to getting a CLT off the ground, as is ensuring that community members see themselves represented in the CLT leadership, says Boyd. “[And] you have to be willing to change and really meet people where they are and not be afraid to make good trouble.” Learn more about Smoketown Community Land Trust here , or get additional information from Grounded Solutions here . Keeping it cool one roof at a time When Tony Chaves noticed how extreme heat and rising air-conditioning costs were affecting his Las Vegas neighborhood, he decided to help solve the problem with a ladder and a bucket of ultra-reflective white paint. As part of the two-person nonprofit Alchemical Opus, Chavez started painting the roofs of Arts District businesses for free, significantly decreasing their indoor temperatures, with one business owner reporting saving $60 to $70 a month on electricity. Coating roofs in white paint is an easy way to lower the temperatures of homes and public buildings. In recent years homeowners across India, Burkina Faso, Mexico and South Pacific have painted their roofs white as part of a global scientific study, with early results indicating substantial cooling. In the U.S., Philadelphia gave 62 households free cool-roof coatings in a 2025 pilot project, while the New York City CoolRoofs program has painted over 12 million square feet of roofs with reflective white paint since 2007. A number of U.S. cities also require cool roofs on new and re-roofed buildings. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The science behind the idea is straightforward: White and reflective roofs absorb less solar heat, and applying reflective coatings is the easiest way to transform a roof into a so-called “cool roof,” while also prolonging the life of the roof . The U.S. Department of Energy says cool roofs can reduce annual air-conditioning energy use in single-story buildings by up to 15 percent, while other studies show that painted roofs can lower maximum indoor temperatures by 2.2 to 5.9°F in residential buildings that are not air conditioned. Learn more about cool roofs here . Housing across generations After moving from the countryside to Vienna for university, Lukas Hecke, Manuel Schuler and Marlene Welzl experienced first-hand how difficult it could be to find good housing on a student budget. At the same time, they knew the city was full of elderly people with small pensions and large apartments, who often felt lonely after their children grew up and moved out. In 2015 they started connecting older people with spare rooms to younger people looking for a place to live. It began organically, by word of mouth, and soon grew into the housing platform Wohnbuddy that has carefully matched over 400 people based on their interests and communications over the years. The impact goes beyond private homes. Since 2017, Wohnbuddy has also partnered with senior residences, where students bring new energy through activities, music and social interaction. Learn more about Wohnbuddy here . The post The Spark: When Communities Own the Land, Housing Stays Affordable appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Congo Basin Peatlands Gets a Scientific Boost Reading Time: 3 minutes A major research collection on African tropical peatlands provides new scientific backing for protecting Congo Basin peatlands and strengthens UNEP’s conservation efforts. A major research collection published in September provides new scientific backing for protecting Congo Basin peatlands . The special issue, released in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, brings together studies on the ecology, hydrology, and social dimensions of African tropical peatlands. Much of the research centers on the Cuvette Centrale, the vast peat swamp spanning the Republic of Congo and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Scientists first mapped the full extent of these peatlands in 2017, revealing a wetland larger than England hidden deep in the Congo Basin’s swamp forests. Researchers estimated the area holds roughly 30 billion metric tons of carbon, an amount comparable to about three years of global fossil fuel emissions. That discovery reshaped how researchers think about tropical peatlands’ role in regulating the planet’s carbon cycle. Keeping that carbon locked underground depends entirely on the peat staying wet. Drainage, agricultural conversion, or sustained drought could release large amounts of stored carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands therefore hinges less on stopping any single threat and more on preserving the hydrological conditions that keep the peat intact. The new research collection highlights how much remains unknown about these dynamics. Contributors point to persistent gaps in understanding how the peatlands might respond to future shifts in rainfall, temperature, and land use. Closing those gaps has become a priority for governments and international partners working across the region. International attention around the peatlands has grown steadily since their 2017 discovery. In 2018, the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Indonesia signed a joint declaration committing to protect their peatlands from unregulated development. The agreement built on momentum from the Global Peatlands Initiative, which has pushed peatland protection higher on the global policy agenda. That cooperation extends beyond the three signatory countries themselves. Researchers and policymakers from outside the region have increasingly framed protecting Congo Basin peatlands as a shared international responsibility, given how much global climate stability depends on keeping the carbon in place. Scientific exchange between African, European, and Asian institutions has become a regular feature of that ongoing collaboration. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands has evolved into a shared international responsibility, with the Republic of Congo, DRC, and Indonesia’s 2018 joint declaration and growing scientific collaboration between African, European, and Asian institutions reflecting global recognition that the climate stability of the entire planet depends on keeping this carbon in the ground. Photo courtesy of the UN Environment Programme . Much of the scientific groundwork behind that cooperation comes from research programs such as CongoPeat, led by the University of Leeds. The project has mapped peat extent and carbon stocks across the central Congo Basin while studying how the ecosystem has formed and changed over thousands of years. That evidence base now feeds directly into regional conservation planning. Translating that science into action falls largely to the Congo Basin Landscapes Initiative, a UNEP-led effort working with regional governments and partners. Within that framework, a dedicated peatlands project backed by Germany’s International Climate Initiative is supporting work in the Lac Télé–Lac Tumba landscape. The project represents nearly €15 million in funding between 2022 and 2027. One tool developed under the project models how different development and climate scenarios could affect water levels and carbon storage across the landscape. Results consistently point to the same conclusion: altering drainage patterns carries real risks for the carbon locked in peat. That finding reinforces why protecting Congo Basin peatlands depends so heavily on careful land-use planning. Research led by the University of Leeds shows the peatlands remain mostly intact today, though threats from road building, logging, and resource extraction continue to grow around their edges. Keeping that intact status will require sustained funding and coordination well beyond any single research project or funding cycle. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands adds another layer of evidence to that ongoing effort rather than offering a final answer. Protecting one of the world’s largest carbon stores will continue to depend on scientists, governments, and local communities working from the same shared body of knowledge. For the Congo Basin, that sustained collaboration may matter as much as any single policy or funding commitment. The post Protecting Congo Basin Peatlands Gets a Scientific Boost appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A surprising new study suggests that an anti-aging drug could help protect people genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's disease. Researchers found that just four weeks of low-dose rapamycin improved brain blood flow in healthy middle-aged adults carrying the high-risk APOE4 gene variant, with women showing the strongest benefits. Because declining blood flow can occur years before Alzheimer's symptoms appear, the discovery raises hopes for preventing or delaying the disease before memory loss begins.

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Κάθε πρωί στον καταυλισμό στο Teknaf, στο Μπαγκλαντές, ο Mohammed Saber ανεβαίνει στην οροφή του σπιτιού της οικογένειάς του από μπαμπού και μουσαμά και τοποθετεί ένα ενιαίο ορθογώνιο ηλιακό πάνελ. Το έκανε αυτό για έξι χρόνια, από τότε που η οικογένειά του διέφυγε από την καταστολή των Ροχίνγκια από τον στρατό της Μιανμάρ το 2017. «Μπορούμε τώρα να χρεώσουμε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every morning in the camp at Teknaf, Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo-and-tarpaulin home and sets out a single rectangular solar panel. He has done this for six years, since his family fled the Myanmar military’s crackdown on the Rohingya people in 2017. “We can now charge our phones, cook with light, children can study at night and use fans during the hot season,” says Saber, 35. A small panel on a makeshift roof, and an entire household runs on it. The same thing is happening in camps and disaster zones around the world. Solar has been edging into humanitarian response for years; what’s shifted is how seriously organizations are taking it, less as an experiment and more as something people actually need. From lanterns to cook stoves The range of what “solar kit” means is wider than it might sound. Sarah Rosenberg-Jansen , a research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute , describes the category as spanning solar lanterns, torches, and heating pads to full solar home systems and electric cook stoves . The common thread is portability and independence from the grid, which matters most when infrastructure is gone and things are moving fast. “In emergency situations , solar kits can be deployed immediately,” she says. That’s playing out across multiple places at once. In Karachi, Doctors Without Borders runs a tuberculosis clinic on solar power. In South Sudan’s Renk County , the UN migration agency installed solar-powered water filtration for families displaced by the war in neighboring Sudan. When Nepal’s floods killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing in August, local and international organizations distributed solar kits to survivors cut off from the grid. In Ukraine, a nonprofit called Hope For Ukraine has provided kits to thousands of families living through a war, including older residents who adapted without trouble. “We have grandmas and grandpas who are around 75 to 80 years old receiving kits,” says CEO Yuriy Boyechko. “It’s just a matter of plug and play.” Why costs finally shifted Solar panels don’t carry the same price volatility as fossil fuels, which are expensive and difficult to transport into disaster zones under ordinary circumstances and near-impossible when infrastructure has been destroyed. Only a few decades ago, solar was a luxury technology. Mass manufacturing and steady advances in efficiency changed that, and the price drop put solar kits within reach of humanitarian budgets in ways they weren’t before. Funding cuts and the waiting list What’s slowing things down now isn’t the technology. Aid organizations have long-running contracts built around diesel generators, and switching to solar means trusting new equipment, building new distribution chains, and sometimes doing that in genuinely hazardous conditions. Mark Gibson of the Global Platform for Action , a group promoting clean energy access, notes that the transition has been complicated for organizations with established logistics in place. Cuts to international donor funding have made it harder. Aimee Jenks, a program leader at GPA, was direct: “Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut. That’s now retracting a lot of progress.” Hope For Ukraine’s own numbers show how stretched the system is. By the end of 2026, the organization expects to have distributed more than 3,200 solar kits, a number that took two years to reach because of funding. “We have a waiting list of about 20,000 families,” Boyechko says. “We just cannot keep up with demand.” For Saber, the gap between what’s available and what people have isn’t an abstraction. His family has had their panel for six years, long enough to know exactly what changed. “It’s improved my family’s life,” he says. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post Solar kits are changing what disaster relief looks like first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Το βρετανικό Pop-Up "Flower Pharmacy" συνταγογραφούσε μπουκέτα που τονώνουν τη διάθεση
items.titleOriginal: UK’s Pop-Up “Flower Pharmacy” Prescribed Mood-Boosting Bouquets
items.description: Το πρώτο «Φαρμακείο λουλουδιών» του Ηνωμένου Βασιλείου άνοιξε τις πόρτες του τον περασμένο μήνα — συνταγογραφώντας ανθοδέσμες αντί για φάρμακα σε όσους χρειάζονται ενίσχυση της διάθεσης. Η μοναδική εμπειρία στο Λονδίνο σχεδιάστηκε για να ενθαρρύνει τους ανθρώπους να σκέφτονται διαφορετικά για τα λουλούδια, δείχνοντας πώς μπορούν να διαδραματίσουν ρόλο στην καθημερινή ευημερία και όχι απλώς να δεσμεύονται για γενέθλια, anniv…
items.descriptionOriginal: The U.K.’s first “Flower Pharmacy” opened its doors last month — prescribing bouquets instead of medicine to those in need of a mood boost. The one-off experience in London was designed to encourage people to think differently about flowers, showing how they can play a role in everyday well-being rather than just being reserved for birthdays, anniversaries, and other special occasions. It was created in partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland and chartered horticulturist, TV gardener, and author David Domoney. Guests were matched with blooms tailored to their mood before leaving with a bouquet recommended to lift, calm, or energize them. For example, yellow flowers, including sunflowers, roses, freesias, and snapdragons, were prescribed to boost happiness, while calming bouquets featured blue and green blooms like hydrangeas, delphiniums, and chrysanthemums. For those who needed a dose of energy, there were also vibrant orange, red, and pink flowers. Courtesy of SWNS The event came as a poll of 2,000 British adults found 37% struggle when daylight saving time ends, with 29% admitting the time change leaves them feeling glum. Discussing the partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, which commissioned the research and the pop-up, Domoney said: “There’s something incredibly uplifting about flowers, and research has shown that they can have a positive effect on our mood and emotional well-being. From the cheerful yellows of sunflowers and freesias to the calming tones of blues and greens, color can influence how we experience the spaces around us.” “We often associate flowers with special occasions, but there’s no reason we shouldn’t enjoy their beauty and the benefits of having them around us in everyday life,” he continued. “Sometimes, it’s the simplest connections with nature that can make a real difference to how we feel.” Courtesy of SWNS The survey also found that around a third of respondents spend more time indoors following the clock change, while 28% find the darker evenings difficult and 22% experience lower energy levels. The good news? There are plenty of ways to lift that low mood, like listening to music, reading a book, exercising, spending time in nature and, yes, buying flowers. While just 9% of people said they regularly treat themselves to blooms, the emotional response to receiving them is clear — half said they feel happy after being presented with a bouquet, 45% grateful, 34% joyful, and 24% comforted. Courtesy of SWNS Monique Kemperman, horticulture expert for Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, said: “As the days become shorter and darker, small acts of self-care can make a real difference, and flowers are a simple way to bring color, joy, and positivity into everyday life.” “Our research shows just how much of an emotional impact they can have, yet many people still reserve them for somebody else or a special occasion,” she added. “The Flower Pharmacy is about encouraging people to see flowers as an everyday well-being boost rather than a treat.” This article was originally written by Jasmine Lenthall for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

Οι περισσότερες τράπεζες τροφίμων και κιτ σούπας…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of motivation that kicks in around the holidays. You think: this year, I’m going to do something. You picture yourself in an apron at a soup kitchen, and it feels good. The problem is that a lot of other people are picturing the same thing at the same time. Most food banks and soup kitchens see volunteer demand spike around Thanksgiving , sometimes to the point where they have more help than they can use on that one day. If you want your time to count, a little strategy goes a long way. The good news: there are 17 solid options below, and several of them work whether you have four hours, four minutes, or no desire to leave your couch. National organizations with locations near you These programs operate across all 50 states, so wherever you are, there’s likely a chapter close enough to walk in. Feeding America Feeding America runs the largest hunger-relief network in the country. If you want to volunteer at a food bank on Thanksgiving, call ahead first. Holiday demand often fills slots fast, and some locations redirect walk-ins toward future dates when the need is more consistent. Meals on Wheels Meals on Wheels delivers hot meals to seniors who can’t get out on their own. The flexibility here is part of the appeal: you can sign up for a single delivery route or build it into a regular habit. The Salvation Army The Salvation Army works across a wide range of needs, from veterans to abuse survivors to people experiencing homelessness. There’s almost always something useful you can do, even on short notice. Operation Turkey Operation Turkey runs a tightly organized four-hour shift from 8 a.m. to noon, packing meals for homeless individuals. If you want a defined commitment with a clear end time, this is a good fit. Feed My Starving Children Feed My Starving Children packs meals at permanent sites in Arizona, Illinois, Minnesota, and Texas. It runs on a reservation system, so sign up before the week of. Toys for Tots Toys for Tots runs its drives through December, so Thanksgiving week is peak season. Volunteer slots exist for collection drives, not just drop-offs. Goodwill Goodwill often looks for people who can share a professional skill, not just sort donations. If you have a background in workforce development, finance, or career coaching, that’s where you’d fit in. United Way United Way sponsors a range of community initiatives, including garden planting, literacy programs, and neighborhood projects. What’s available depends on your city, so look up your local chapter. Local options that don’t require a national signup Soup kitchens and community meal programs often run on the same skeleton crew year after year. A call a week ahead is usually all it takes. Animal shelters are another option, especially if you’re better with dogs than crowds. Staff still work on Thanksgiving, and extra hands for walks or socialization are usually welcome. If you’re up for something more active, turkey trots are 5K races held in communities across the country on Thanksgiving morning, with proceeds going to local charities. You walk or run, and the entry fee does the work. The National Park Service also coordinates trail maintenance and cleanup projects throughout the fall. Check the volunteer page for your nearest park. If you can’t leave the house Gift-a-Family Gift-a-Family lets you sponsor a family through their holiday wishlist. The sign-up deadline is November 30, so there’s still time. Homefront America Homefront America directs donations toward grocery and turkey vouchers for military families. Support Our Troops Support Our Troops coordinates handwritten letters to deployed service members. It takes about ten minutes and goes a long way. One thing to know before you go Holiday volunteering is genuinely good, but the reality is that organizations often need year-round help. Of course, showing up once during the holidays could be the gateway to showing up regularly. If you get redirected on Thanksgiving Day because a food bank is at capacity, ask when they need people most. Often the answer is right after the holiday rush! Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: T he staff at Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has a saying: Sheets, towels and lives changed daily . Erik’s Ranch is a guest retreat where autistic people are concierges, guides, wranglers, cooks and more. Located on 230 acres of pristine pasture and wilderness near Livingston, Montana, the ranch is less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park. It offers horseback riding, fly fishing, nature hikes, history walks and experiences with ranch animals and wildlife — most led or assisted by paid neurodivergent “members,” most of whom also live on the property. The inspiration for Erik’s Ranch dates back to 2008, when founder Kathryn Nordberg was pondering how her son, Erik, whom she described as “a moderately functioning teenager with autism,” would live as an adult — and particularly what would happen when she was no longer around. Ranch manager Cameron Porter (in black hat) and member John Rekedal help a visitor from New Jersey mount her steed for a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen “As someone challenged with expressive language, there weren’t very many opportunities for kids like him,” she said, sitting in the well-appointed kitchen of the ranch’s six-bedroom lodge. So she established a nonprofit with a boutique-style hotel in Edina, Minnesota, where, even after she’s gone, Erik and others like him can live, work and thrive. There, adults on the autism spectrum work and live independently and are guided by life coaches toward achieving personal goals like interviewing, equine or cooking skills; or setting up an Etsy page to sell their artwork. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Using a similar model, in 2014 Nordberg opened the Montana ranch, where not only employees on the spectrum benefit: She designed most of the cabins specifically for neurodivergent guests. Though anyone can appreciate the soothing atmosphere, it’s particularly accommodating for those on the spectrum, who sometimes experience sensory overload. The calmingly simple cabins provide awe-inspiring vistas of the surrounding mountains with little to no sign of human activity. Hardware was selected to close drawers, cabinets and doors with hardly a sound. Walls, furnishings and bedding are muted earth tones and lights have dimmers. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch is run primarily by young autistic people, some of whom also live on the property. The ranch has unparalleled views of the Absaroka-Beartooth Mountains. Autistic and other neurodivergent people are often misunderstood and feel out-of-place, experiencing discrimination, social exclusion, bullying and other situations that can lead to low self-esteem. That — and an inexorable need to mask their differences — often results in depression and anxiety. Some studies indicate that people on the spectrum are four times more likely to experience major depression compared with the general population. “Depression, loneliness, lack of confidence, feeling isolated, rejected, and a lack of community and people who care is what Erik’s Ranch is working to minimize and eliminate,” Nordberg said. And it’s working. John Rekedal, 21, lives in Minnesota but just spent his first summer working at the Montana ranch. When he’s home, he works in a large production greenhouse. And though his coworkers there are understanding, he prefers the camaraderie of working with the ranch’s small staff amid the hush of the surrounding mountains. Jacob Thoresen fetches horses from a pasture in preparation for a trail ride. Thoresen has been working for Erik’s Ranch and Retreats for 10 years. Credit: Jodi Hausen “I’m a whole lot more inclined to work outside,” he said. “And I know everyone’s name. It’s more relaxed.” Cornell University autism researcher Leslie Shaw analyzed a national sample of autistic adults who could answer a survey unassisted and found that only about 53 percent were working in 2023. Furthermore, in 2024, people with cognitive disabilities (of which neurodivergence is a subset) were employed at less than half the rate of people without any disability, according to Cornell’s Northeast ADA Center . These low employment rates may be due to neurotypical employers’ lack of experience with and understanding of neurodivergent people leading to misaligned work assignments, confusion and a fraught or untenable work environment. On a recent late summer day in Montana, Jacob Thoresen, 33, was gearing up to lead a small group of guests on a trail ride. He has been working with the nonprofit for 10 years and splits his time between its two locations. In black cowboy hat and jeans, he walked back and forth across the dirt-floored indoor arena to a tack room, gathering saddles and bridles. He saddled horses while other members dutifully scooped and cleaned areas around the animals. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch & Retreats is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. Thoresen had other jobs before coming to Erik’s. He was a baggage handler at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul Airport and worked in retail and manufacturing. He even tried a desk job. “But,” he said with a smile, “that isn’t me.” Thoresen said he’s gained confidence working with Erik’s Ranch & Retreats. “If you would have met me 10 years ago, I would have been, like, I couldn’t be able to do anything independent and be trusted to actually get the work done,” he said. “This place is teaching me how to be independent. In this last year, I’ve grown more.” He still gets support, but staff, recognizing his achievements, have loosened the reins. “I’m having to rely more on myself to work on those independent skills,” he added. Hannah Jacobs (left) helps Zoe Markman put fresh linens on a bed in one of the guest cabins at Erik’s Ranch. Credit: Jodi Hausen When asked what he finds challenging about working at Erik’s Ranch, Thoresen said workdays can be inconsistent. At the Minnesota retreat, he completes the same tasks daily. On the ranch, daily schedules shift and sometimes he gets overwhelmed. “But I can move through it,” he said. “I attribute that to the staff that I work with and just practice. They do a good job of seeing [my overwhelm] and being like, okay. And that helps, you know. I’ve had too many employers in the past that have been like, ‘Oh, you’re not having a good day? Well, just go home.’” Over the years, Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has employed 27 autistic young adults — 19 in the last year. The goal, Nordberg said, is to serve 30 members regularly. The organization is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. John Rekedal helps clean around the horses in the indoor arena before a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen Not far from Erik’s Ranch, Special K Ranch in Columbus, Montana, provides living quarters and jobs in farming, ranching and gardening and contracts with area businesses to employ adults with developmental disabilities. Over in Jackson, Wyoming, Vertical Harvest integrates people with a wide array of disabilities into their operations growing lettuces, microgreens, tomatoes and basil. In a fully accessible greenhouse, Vertical Harvest operates on what’s known as the “Grow Well” model of employment : providing opportunities for workers to pursue passions by creating or placing them in positions that correspond to their strengths and aspirations, their likes and dislikes. In other words, adapting the workplace to the employee rather than the other way around. Although she hadn’t heard of Grow Well, Nordberg embraces its philosophy. It doesn’t always work out as planned, though. “Not everyone wants to learn hospitality,” she said. In fact, one autistic young man told her he wanted to be a “white hat hacker,” using his computer skills for good. But she didn’t have a role that fit his skills and aspirations. In other instances, however, a member’s passions can be integrated into ranch operations. Part-time member Zoe Markman shows off a colorful collection of eggs gathered from the hens in the coop behind her. Credit: Jodi Hausen Zoe Markman, a 21-year-old autistic woman from Bozeman, loves animals — particularly chickens. So when Markman started working part-time at the ranch, Nordberg built a chicken coop and populated it with more than a dozen hens whom Markman gave punny names: Chiquille O’Neal, Princess Layer and Hen Solo. On a recent workday, Markman gathered more than a dozen colorful eggs. Nordberg also helped Erik start a baking business making cookies, brownies, scones and banana bread. Erik is a visual learner and communicator, so Nordberg created a pictorial cookbook with step-by-step instructions. She marked bins of flour, sugar and other ingredients with pictures so Erik can do most of the work independently. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The ranch can currently house five members and has five cabins and the lodge for guests on its expansive property. So Nordberg has room to expand, and she’d like to. But finances and land-use regulations present barriers. It’s expensive running a guest ranch, though the costs are partly covered by guest fees and philanthropy. And area permitting will only allow for seven more cabins. “This will never be a huge operation,” Nordberg said. But she’s gratified knowing there are places for Erik and others like him to live, belong and find meaningful work. This story was supported in part by the Solutions Journalism Network’s HEAL Fellowship. The post The Montana Ranch Where Autistic People Are Wranglers and Guides appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Sewage is full of organic matter that can be a source of energy. But it also carries harmful chemicals as well as leftover medicines that conventional treatment methods can’t remove easily. Researchers now report a technology that can solve three sewage-related problems at the same time. Their new device uses bacteria in wastewater to generate electricity while breaking down a hard-to-degrade antibiotic and producing a valuable industrial chemical. The team published their results in Journal of Power Sources . There have been plenty of research efforts to harness microbes for treating wastewater while producing renewable energy. The approach uses microbial fuel cells , which are battery-like devices with two electrodes. In microbial fuel cells, bacteria grow on an electrode and devour organic matter , converting chemical energy into electrons, which flow in an external circuit to produce electricity. Then those electrons meet oxygen at the other electrode to create water. Turns out that microbial fuel cells usually generate very small amounts of electricity. “So we asked a different question: What else could those electrons do when they arrive?,” writes the team from hydrogen peroxide instead of water. Hydrogen peroxide is a household chemical used for disinfection and bleaching. It is also used widely in chemical manufacturing. The chemical industry makes it today using an energy- and chemical-intensive process in large plants. To get the right reaction in the microbial fuel cell, the researchers designed a new electrode. They embedded iron and nickel oxides on a flexible carbon fiber cloth. When they heated the cloth in the presence of acetylene at 800°C, a forest of carbon nanofibers grew out of it. “The metal particles rode the growing fibers upward, so every fiber ended with a metal oxide tip,” the researchers say. So the electrode has conductive fibers with a catalytic tip. And bacteria cling to this rough conductive surface and form a thick film. The team used the same electrodes on both side of the fuel cell. When they ran sewage spiked with the antibiotic chloramphenicol through the cell, it removed 99.99% of the drug while producing hydrogen peroxide in two days. “Next, we plan to run it longer, test other drugs, check the toxicity of the breakdown products and link several cells in series to raise the power,” the team writes. “So can dirty water help pay for its own cleanup? Not completely yet. But in two days, our system turned sewage into cleaner water, a useful chemical and a little electricity.” Source : Yashmeen Budania et al. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes Across 3 million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon, protecting forests from disturbance delivered greater biodiversity benefits than restoring already-cleared land, according to new research comparing conservation strategies. Conservation policy has long debated where limited funding should go: preventing deforestation outright, protecting standing forests from degradation, or restoring land already cleared. A study published in Science this September provides the clearest answer yet, using counterfactual scenarios built from observed land-use changes across three million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon’s deforestation frontier. Led by Leonardo S. Miranda of Lancaster University alongside researchers including Joice Ferreira of Embrapa, the team compared three intervention types against what actually happened on the ground. Protecting forests from disturbance, meaning avoiding fire and selective logging within standing forest, reduced biodiversity loss by 68.5% and carbon loss by 46.8% compared with the baseline scenario. Avoiding deforestation entirely mitigated 60.8% of carbon loss and 28.0% of biodiversity loss. Restoration of already-cleared land delivered the smallest gains for both outcomes. These findings challenge a common assumption in conservation funding, where restoration often receives outsized attention and investment despite standing forests requiring protection first. Protecting forests from disturbance proved nearly as effective as preventing deforestation for carbon storage, while substantially outperforming it for biodiversity outcomes, a distinction with direct implications for how governments and conservation organizations allocate resources. Neither single intervention alone reversed losses across the landscape. Combining avoided deforestation with protection from disturbance was necessary to achieve net-positive outcomes, increasing biodiversity by 12% and carbon by 18% above 2010 baseline levels. This combined approach proved essential precisely because deforestation and forest degradation operate through different mechanisms, requiring complementary rather than substitutable responses. Restoration still carries genuine value, particularly in landscapes where deforestation has already progressed extensively. The research team found that restoration delivered meaningful benefits, particularly on properties where much of the original forest cover had already disappeared, suggesting it works best as a complement to protection rather than a replacement. Protecting forests from disturbance addresses threats that often receive less policy attention than outright deforestation. Selective logging removes valuable timber species while leaving forest canopy nominally intact, and wildfires increasingly penetrate forest edges weakened by fragmentation and drought. Both processes degrade forest structure, reduce habitat quality for forest-dependent species, and release stored carbon, yet they generate far less public attention than visible clear-cutting. Protecting forests from disturbance targets fire and selective logging, threats that degrade forest structure without clear-cutting, with researchers finding that combined deforestation and disturbance avoidance are necessary to achieve net-positive biodiversity and carbon outcomes above 2010 baseline levels. Photo by Bill Salazar on Pexels. The study’s timing is especially urgent as climate change intensifies. The research team noted that combined interventions become increasingly important as warming progresses, since forest restoration efforts prove particularly vulnerable to wildfire risk. Newly planted or naturally regenerating young forests lack the structural resilience of mature canopies, making restoration investments vulnerable to being undone by the same fire disturbances the study identifies as critical to prevent. This vulnerability creates a policy challenge extending well beyond Brazil. As governments and international organizations increasingly emphasize forest restoration within climate commitments and biodiversity frameworks, protecting forests from disturbance offers a complementary message: restoration investments achieve far less impact when the remaining standing forest around them continues degrading from fire and logging. Joice Ferreira, principal investigator of the Capoeira restoration research program at Embrapa, emphasized that restoration remains essential precisely where forests have been lost across large areas, reinforcing that the study’s findings don’t diminish restoration’s role but rather clarify where and when it delivers the strongest returns. Restoration works best as part of integrated strategies rather than as a primary tool used independently of forest protection efforts. The research methodology itself offers a template for conservation planning elsewhere. By using observed land-use changes to construct counterfactual scenarios, the team measured what would have happened under different intervention choices and quantified trade-offs that previous studies could only estimate qualitatively. This approach allows policymakers to weigh cost-effectiveness directly rather than relying on intuition about which conservation strategy delivers the greatest return per dollar invested. As tropical deforestation frontiers worldwide face similar pressures from fire, logging, and agricultural expansion, protecting forests from disturbance provides an evidence-based framework extending beyond the Brazilian Amazon alone. The findings suggest that conservation funding achieves maximum impact not through any single strategy in isolation, but through carefully sequenced combinations addressing deforestation, degradation, and restoration simultaneously, each targeting the specific threats most relevant to a given landscape’s current condition. The post Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: For centuries, the sacred groves of Rajasthan were understood as human gifts to nature -- places where belief drew a boundary and the forest was allowed to breathe. But as this essay quietly argues, the order of that story is wrong: people protected a handful of fig trees, and the birds did everything else. The peepal, the banyan, the gular -- three figs that tradition placed beyond the reach of the axe - fed birds through every lean season, and those birds, carrying seeds from across the landscape, built the grove outward from that protected center, generation after generation. "What belief really preserved was a process," the author writes, "a place where the planting could go on undisturbed for centuries." There is something worth sitting with in that realization: that the deepest acts of protection are often for something we cannot fully see, and that what looks like a tree standing alone is, if the birds still come, a forest in the making.
