items.descriptionOriginal: A former Los Angeles gang member, a former skinhead and a former radical Islamist walk into a youth center. What sounds like the setup for an uneasy joke is at the core of Farah Pandith’s work: Put people who might otherwise never share a room in front of young people; let them explain what drew them into extremism and how they found their way out. “They’re the most authentic and credible voices there are,” Pandith says. More than once she has observed that their stories reach an audience that official warnings cannot. For decades, including while working for the U.S. government under the Obama, George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush administrations, Pandith researched why people embrace ideologies that divide the world into “us versus them.” Before people can be persuaded away from hatred, she argues, one has to understand what they are looking for: recognition, certainty or a place in the world. “You don’t suddenly explode and become an extremist overnight. You’re having some self-doubt, you’re asking questions about who you are,” she says from her light-filled living room in Arlington, Virginia. Preventing someone from becoming an extremist has been her lifelong goal, because it’s “infinitely easier than dealing with the fallout.” Farah Pandith visits the Indonesian city of Bekasi during her time as the U.S. special representative to Muslim communities. Credit: U.S. Embassy, Jakarta / Wikimedia Commons While working for the government, she traveled to nearly 100 countries, from Belgium to Bangladesh, to understand how extremists’ descent into violence can be interrupted. Today she applies what she learned to a broader problem: how to make compassion more than an admirable sentiment and help communities put it into practice. Last year Pandith received the ADL Daniel Pearl Award , which is given annually to a person who has had a positive impact on understanding between Jews and the Muslim world, and is sponsored by the parents of the journalist who was kidnapped and killed in Pakistan in 2002. “It is hard to think of anyone more knowledgeable than Farah Pandith when it comes to countering violent extremism,” Joseph Nye, the late chair of the National Intelligence Council, said about her. On September 11, 2001, Pandith watched on television like millions of others as two planes struck the World Trade Center. “It felt very heavy,” she recalls, putting a hand to her heart. “The world kind of went still for a moment, like, ‘What do we do about this?’” She felt compelled to act, to help prevent such violence from happening again. She especially rejected the way extremists attempted to define her religion on the airwaves. “Who are they to dictate what Islam is?” she remembers thinking. “For me, Islam means humility, compassion, to treat others with respect.” Initially, when she worked for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), cooperating with local organizations showed her that effective policy depends on understanding the people on the ground. “You have to listen really well to find a solution that matches with the local community,” she says. “That’s tricky and complex. Trust has to be built first.” The same principle, she realized, applied to preventing violent extremism. Government officials could not design effective strategies from Washington alone. They needed to hear from the people they hoped to reach, including those whose voices had been overlooked. After joining the National Security Council in 2004, Pandith helped develop the “soft power” side of the Global War on Terror through a new approach called Countering Violent Extremism. Military action might disrupt extremist organizations, but it could not prevent them from recruiting new members. Nor were public relations campaigns successful in overcoming the distrust of Muslims worldwide. Even in her own government, distrust was impossible to ignore. One congressman called the White House to complain a “jihadist” was sitting in the Council. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Pandith was briefly living in Afghanistan’s capital, Kabul, in 2004 when photographs of abuse at Abu Ghraib surfaced showing American soldiers humiliating Muslim prisoners. “In an instant, all our efforts on the ground were harmed irreparably,” she says. Locals asked how she could represent a government that treated Muslim prisoners that way. The experience reinforced a lesson: Building trust also meant receiving criticism, sitting through uncomfortable conversations. Pandith carried that approach into her work at the State Department, where Hillary Clinton appointed her the first U.S. special representative to Muslim communities in 2009. Instead of treating Muslim populations as a single audience for American messages, she traveled widely, meeting people in homes, mosques and community settings to learn what mattered to them. “You have to go to the rural areas,” she says, aiming to support credible local voices that could offer alternatives to extremist narratives. Pandith herself has been shaped by a background that made her an ideal diplomat. She came to the U.S. from Kashmir as a baby with her mother, a pulmonologist and the medical director of a hospital. Pandith describes growing up in a highly educated Muslim family without experiencing discrimination. She remembers an America in which people of different faiths could live alongside one another, “with a synagogue, a church, a mosque and a temple in the same part of town.” Today, she admits, that harmonious coexistence feels nearly impossible. Her parents separated when she was 10, and her mother raised Pandith and her brother on her own. One of her greatest influences was her uncle, a heart surgeon. “I’ve held the hearts of different people in my hands,” he would tell her. “Always remember: There is no difference between the heart of a Muslim, a Jew, a Hindu or a Christian.” Pandith feels she carries “many identities” — an American, a woman, a Muslim and a foreign policy professional, among others. While traveling as Special Representative to Muslim Communities in the Obama administration, she said she had a “superpower” when speaking with Muslims. When she told them she was born in Srinagar in Kashmir, India, the atmosphere often changed. “Suddenly I’m like a sister to them.” Farah Pandith on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit. Courtesy of Farah Pandith Her ability to forge connections would become one of her greatest professional assets. By chance, Barbara Bush, the wife of President George H.W. Bush, visited Smith College during Farah’s senior year. She was so impressed by a speech Pandith gave as student body president that she helped her secure her job at USAID after graduation. That was how the young woman began traveling around the world. Pandith’s work challenged conventional explanations of radicalization. Poverty and lack of education, she argued, could not explain why people embraced violent ideologies. Some of the 9/11 terrorists were well educated. Pandith pointed to a different cause she observed in Muslim communities: deep identity crises among young people who struggled to find their place in a rapidly changing world. She thinks of a young woman in Denmark whose Imam told her she wasn’t a Muslim if she didn’t cover her head. Or Mubin Shaikh in Canada, who went to Pakistan and Syria as a 19-year-old to fight alongside the jihadists and who now teaches security politics at the University of Ottawa. Pandith has seen firsthand that dialogue can change minds. ““It’s less interesting for the media than an extremist’s video, but the conversations we had affected people.” Her initiatives have sought to make dialogue a shared responsibility. Against Violent Extremism became the world’s first and only network of former extremists, launched by the U.S. Department of State, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and Google. The “Hours Against Hate” campaign encouraged teenagers to spend an hour doing something for someone different from themselves. Millions participated. Sisters Against Violent Extremism connected mothers concerned about their children’s vulnerability to extremist recruitment. In a citizen-dialogue program, Pandith traveled through Europe with other Muslim Americans to share experiences and listen to local concerns. People had the chance to meet someone they might otherwise see only through stereotypes and to develop a relationship that complicated those assumptions. In her book How We Win , recently reissued, Pandith remains stubbornly optimistic: The fight against extremism can be won. Preventing people from being drawn into extremist movements requires intervening early and bringing together the people who can reach them — not just government officials, but business leaders, teachers, local communities and influencers whose networks, knowledge and credibility government agencies lack. “The fight against violent extremism is not going to be won solely by the efforts of government,” she argues. “We need businesses to step up as never before, for the public interest as well as their own.” She insists that this work cannot be dismissed as idealism or do-goodery but is “a matter of national security” — as important as the hard power of military force. Pandith emphasizes that the underlying lessons can be relevant for many communities. The same dynamics of exclusion and dehumanization can fuel hostility toward religious minorities, LGBTQ+ people and Asian communities, among others. Still, she admits that the strategies for countering violent extremism never fully came to fruition, often mired in bureaucracy. “Congress provided just 0.0138 percent of funding compared to the funding for the military,” she calculates. “We know what we need to do. We spent 25 years researching and exchanging strategies. But we left the field to the extremists.” Pandith sees the reality as a call to action: “We cannot just wring our hands and keep saying things are bad and things are difficult and somebody else’s problem. We need everybody.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime She now works outside government to advance another part of this agenda, as senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations , teaching countering violent extremism at Georgetown University, and as a Global Peace Laureate for the Muhammad Ali Center. She has been developing the Muhammad Ali Index on compassion . For Pandith, compassion is the capacity to recognize another person’s humanity even amid disagreement, and to resist the impulse to turn differences into a reason for contempt. “There isn’t a faith on planet Earth that doesn’t have compassion in it. And even if you are not religious you understand what it means, right?” As part of the Muhammed Ali Index, more than 5,400 people in 12 American cities responded to the 2025 State of Compassion survey . Sixty-one percent said they felt compassion has declined in the last four years, but 43 percent were optimistic about the future of compassion in America. A second index, planned for 2027, will cover 20 U.S. cities and 12 cities around the world. The ambition is practical. Pandith hopes the data will help mayors, school leaders, faith groups and local organizations identify opportunities to build stronger connections and design efforts suited to their own communities. The point is not to prescribe a universal program, but to create a framework that can be adapted. “We want to see people taking inspiration from the data to actually do something over time so we can measure and see what takes place,” she says passionately, insisting that compassion can be trained: “Compassion is a muscle that can be exercised.” Yet the starting point is personal: “Self-compassion is essential.” Building the capacity for compassion, Pandith argues, begins with recognizing what is happening inside oneself. She is particularly interested in reaching young people early. “The world that they are growing up in is so polarized and so difficult and so different from the one that we have grown up in,” she says, “that they don’t have a memory of people who are different from them speaking to each other with dignity regularly.” As Pandith sees it, waiting for polarization to disappear on its own is not a strategy. The task is to build relationships and connections that open up hearts and minds — and to keep investing in them long enough to learn what works. She repeats her favorite sentence: “Solutions are available and affordable.” UPDATE — November 3, 2026: This story has been updated to clarify facts about Pandith’s work and background. items.descriptionOriginal: Some bees line their nests with soft petals. Some line them with hardened tree sap. Some line them with a thin, flexible film composed of silk and polyester. And this latter group—known as cellophane bees—may hold the key to sustainable, biodegradable plastic, according to a new study. “Nature has already solved a problem that polymer scientists are still working on: a bioplastic that is chemically and physically similar to conventional plastics but doesn’t persist in the environment,” says study team member Jonathan Coote , assistant professor in the Department of Sustainable Biomaterials at Virginia Tech University. Unlike more familiar hive-dwelling honeybees, cellophane bees nest in the soil. Females lay eggs in individual chambers that they line with secretions from a gland on their abdomen. Scientists have known for almost half a century that this lining is composed of silk fibers and a polyester similar to polyethylene—a material that makes up about one-third of human-produced plastics and is the most commonly used plastic for packaging. “Polyethylene-like polyesters made in the lab generally don’t break down well in the environment,” says Coote. “The bees’ material, however, breaks down rapidly in soil.” Although the bees nest in aggregations of 10,000 or more individual nests and often use the same nest sites for decades, their habitat never becomes choked with plastic—in contrast to large aggregations of modern humans. To find out more about how the bees do it, Coote and his collaborators gathered nest linings from two Tennessee nest sites of a species of cellophane bee known as Colletes inaequalis . They put the material through a battery of tests to characterize its structure and chemical makeup. They also collected nest linings that had been in the ground for four, seven, and 11 months to track how the material degrades over time. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby The tradeoff at the heart of bioplastics. A fresh nest cell lining is about 73% polyester and 27% silk by weight, the researchers report. The polyester is semicrystalline, likely has cross-linked polymer chains, and has a crystal structure and degradation temperature similar to that of polyethylene. “The biggest surprise was that the material is most likely cross-linked, meaning its polymer chains are chemically tied together into a network,” says Coote. “Cross-linked plastics, called thermosets, are typically very durable, and designing thermosets that break down at the end of their life is a major challenge in polymer science. So finding a thermoset that breaks down rapidly in soil was very counterintuitive, and it’s exciting to have a natural example to learn from.” By four months, the nest linings are just 40% polyester, meaning that the polyester degrades even more rapidly than famously biodegradable silk in the first months (after that, the composition changes much more slowly). Four-month-old nest linings remain flexible and intact, protecting the nest cell from moisture and microbes like a shrink-wrapped bell pepper at the grocery store. By seven months, about the time the larva has developed into an adult bee, the lining easily cracks easily; by 11 months, it crumbles in the hand. In other words, unlike that bell pepper’s shrink wrap, the nest lining lasts just as long as is needed to protect the developing bee, and no longer. The researchers next aim to investigate how the material breaks down so quickly. They hypothesize that the particularities of polyester’s crystal structure may leave the bonds that connect the material’s subunits exposed to a greater degree than in other polyesters. There’s also evidence of an enzyme that breaks these bonds present in the nest lining, perhaps from the mother bee’s saliva. “The goal is to reverse engineer what the bees are doing so that we can design similar materials in the lab and eventually produce them at practical scale,” Coote says. Source: Coote J.P., et al. “ Rapid soil degradation of a cross-linked, semicrystalline polyethylene-like polyester produced by Colletes bees .” PNAS 2026. Image: Laura Russo.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action Reading Time: 3 minutes Wildlife conservation filmmaking connects audiences with wild places and the people protecting them. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives viewers a reason to care about wild places they may never see in person. Fin and Fur Films , an award-winning production company, builds its work around that idea. Its team focuses on wildlife, adventure, and conservation stories. The company says it is proudest of films that led to real-world conservation impacts. That goal shapes every project. In wildlife conservation filmmaking, a film succeeds when it moves audiences to care, not just when it entertains. Ben Masters, founder and director, started the company in 2012 with a Kickstarter campaign. Kickstarter is an online fundraising platform where many people donate small amounts. That campaign paid for the film Unbranded. Unbranded follows four young cowboys who adopted, trained, and rode a string of wild mustangs 3,000 miles from Mexico to Canada. That is about the distance across the continental United States. The route crossed some of the wildest terrain in the American West. The trip included runaway horses, a sassy donkey, perilous mountain passes, and rodeos. It also brought sickness, injury, and death. The film won the Audience Award at Telluride Mountainfilm and the Hot Docs Film Festival. Unbranded also shines a light on the complex situation facing the country’s wild horses. The adventure holds attention, and the film explains the issue along the way. Wildlife conservation filmmaking often works this way. The River and the Wall takes a similar approach. Five friends travel 1,200 miles from El Paso to the Gulf of Mexico through the unknown wilds of the Texas borderlands. They go by horse, mountain bike, and canoe. That distance equals nearly a full day of nonstop highway driving, but the friends covered it much more slowly. They set out to document the borderlands. They also wanted to explore how a border wall could affect the natural environment. As the wilderness gave way to the more populated Lower Rio Grande Valley, the friends met the human side of the immigration debate. The trip took an emotional turn they had not planned for. Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story brings wildlife conservation filmmaking to an entire state. Actor Matthew McConaughey narrates the visually stunning film. It celebrates Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Wildlife conservation filmmaking comes to an entire state in Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story , narrated by Matthew McConaughey, a visually stunning film celebrating Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Photo courtesy of Fin and Fur Films . The film aims to protect the state’s remaining wild places. It shows how water and wildlife depend on each other. It also recognizes Texas’s important role in conservation across the continent. Reach matters in wildlife conservation filmmaking. Fin and Fur Films has shared its work through Netflix, Apple TV, PBS Nature, Prime, National Geographic, and LoveNature. The films have also appeared in large theatrical releases and on international television. Global Wildlife Conservation notes that well-made environmental documentaries can bring people closer to nature and inspire them to protect it. The Fin and Fur Films catalog shows how that works in practice. Each story pairs a real adventure with a real conservation question. Partnerships help wildlife conservation filmmaking go further. The company has worked with American Rivers, The Nature Conservancy, and Texan by Nature. It has also partnered with brands such as H-E-B and YETI. The numbers show how far a small team can stretch. The company has produced five feature films and more than 30 short films. It has worked with more than 40 conservation groups, which is roughly one partner group per film. See also: A Documentary About Overfishing Sparked Blue Marine Foundation’s Ocean Conservation Mission Masters says the crew keeps its roots as river lovers, backcountry horsemen, and field-savvy wildlife biologists. He also stresses that each film is a team effort. Dozens, or even hundreds, of people contribute to each one. Masters credits partners, collaborators, donors, contractors, and the viewers who give their time to watch. That shared support keeps the work going. Audiences are part of the effort, too. Good stories make conservation feel personal. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives those stories a wide audience. Which wild place would you most like to see protected next? items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns Reading Time: 3 minutes Yuvelis Morales Blanco won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and helping halt two pilot projects and secure a landmark court ruling. A university student began stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns by knocking on her neighbors’ doors. Seven years later, Yuvelis Morales Blanco has won the 2026 Goldman Environmental Prize for that work. The prize honors grassroots environmental leaders from six world regions each year. Her campaign helped stop two pilot fracking projects near her hometown of Puerto Wilches. It also led to a Constitutional Court ruling that upheld her Afro-Colombian community’s right to a say. To date, no fracking project has moved forward anywhere in Colombia. Morales Blanco, now 24, grew up in a family of subsistence fishers on the Magdalena River. The river flows nearly 1,000 miles from the Andes to the Caribbean, about the distance from Boston to Atlanta. For the roughly 30,000 people of Puerto Wilches, it provides food, income, and identity. The town also sits in the heart of Colombia’s oil country. Ecopetrol, the largest and majority state-owned oil company, is based in nearby Barrancabermeja. Between 2015 and 2022, about 40% of its more than 2,000 oil spills happened in this region. That works out to roughly two spills a week for eight years. In 2018, a leak at the Lizama 158 well displaced about 100 families and killed thousands of fish. So when the government proposed fracking nearby, residents had reason to worry. In 2019, then-President Iván Duque announced two pilot projects called Kalé and Platero. Ecopetrol led both, with ExxonMobil as operator and majority partner on Platero. Fracking, short for hydraulic fracturing, pumps water, sand, and chemicals into rock at high pressure. The pressure cracks the rock and frees trapped oil or gas. The process uses large amounts of water and can contaminate rivers and groundwater. Morales Blanco was studying environmental engineering at the time. She paused her degree and began visiting neighbors to explain the risks. She also joined the Alianza Colombia Libre de Fracking, or Colombia Free from Fracking Alliance. With the alliance, she helped lead protests outside the Ecopetrol refinery. In January 2022, she testified at permit hearings and organized a peaceful sit-in. Soon after the sit-in, armed men showed up at her home. She fled Colombia, and France granted her asylum in February 2022. No one has been convicted for the threats against her. Exile in France did not end her campaign. She received the Marianne Initiative award for human rights defenders and raised the issue with President Emmanuel Macron. She also brought the case before the International Rights of Nature Tribunal. Back home, the campaign for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns began winning in court. In April 2022, a court suspended environmental permits for both projects until companies consulted local communities. Months later, newly elected President Gustavo Petro announced his opposition to fracking. Community organizing helped secure a court-ordered suspension of two fracking projects in 2022, a key step in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River, followed months later by President Gustavo Petro’s opposition to fracking. Photo by Christian Escobar Mora courtesy of Goldman Environmental Prize . Ecopetrol suspended the project contracts in September 2022. By November, it had halted Kalé and Platero and undone its agreements with ExxonMobil. The decisive ruling came in August 2024. Colombia’s Constitutional Court found that the pilots violated the community’s right to free, prior, and informed consent. Under this principle, companies must consult communities and win their agreement before projects affect their land. That decision reaches beyond Puerto Wilches. It confirms that Afro-Colombian communities have a legal voice over what happens on their territory. The precedent matters for stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities and anywhere similar projects appear. Morales Blanco has since returned to Puerto Wilches and keeps organizing with the alliance. She describes the Magdalena as the life that sustains her family and her fishing community. She also points out that her region produces great energy wealth while many residents stay poor. The Global Greengrants Fund, which supports the alliance, notes that each prize winner represents a broader movement. More than 80 of the fund’s partners and allies have received the prize since 1993. Afro-Colombian fishing communities stood beside her in stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River towns. Morales Blanco won for the South and Central America region, one of six 2026 winners , all of whom were women. The others came from Nigeria, South Korea, the United Kingdom, Papua New Guinea, and the United States. Colombia’s politics have shifted since her win. President Abelardo de la Espriella took office in August 2026 after campaigning to expand fracking. Still, the 2024 ruling gives communities like Puerto Wilches firm legal ground to demand a say. Stopping fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River communities didn’t require a big budget or political office. It took a young woman who knew her river and kept going after threats forced her abroad. Her prize shows how local action can shape national policy. The post Goldman Prize Honors Young Activist for Stopping Fracking in Colombia’s Magdalena River Towns appeared first on Happy Eco News .
